testing-debugging-tools.p1: Most of this list is talks about writing code that is easy to test and change, recommended as answers to questions that keep coming up. Stack Overflow users link the 2008 Google TechTalks Clean Code series, especially The Clean Code Talks - Global State and Singletons, whenever someone asks why Singletons hurt unit testing. Rails Conf 2013 The Magic Tricks of Testing by Sandi Metz settles arguments about testing private methods and mocks. On Hacker News, TDD, Where Did It All Go Wrong (Ian Cooper) is often called the best talk on testing, and Performance Matters by Emery Berger is the usual reply when a tiny edit shifts a benchmark.
testing-debugging-tools.p2: A sensible first watch is one of the Google Clean Code talks from 2008. Each takes on one narrow question, such as polymorphism versus switch statements or dependency injection, so it stands alone. The bigger commitment is working through the Sandi Metz and Ian Cooper talks together, since they push you to rethink how you test. CppCon 2017's Matt Godbolt talk on reading compiler output and the 2014 Strange Loop talk on deterministic simulation of distributed systems round out the top. Further down are refactoring, profiling and tooling talks.

systems-programming-languages.p1: This list is mostly CppCon talks, with a Go thread from Rob Pike and the Google I/O 2012 talk Go Concurrency Patterns. Most of these work as standing answers to recurring questions. Chandler Carruth's Tuning C++: Benchmarks, and CPUs, and Compilers! Oh My! gets linked whenever a microbenchmark is optimized away. Kate Gregory's Stop Teaching C is the reply to C-style C++ written by beginners. The Nightmare of Initialization in C++ settles arguments about braces versus parentheses. A few, like Andrei Alexandrescu's std::allocator talk, are recommended simply because people found them entertaining and worth rewatching.
systems-programming-languages.p2: A good first watch is Matt Godbolt's What Has My Compiler Done for Me Lately? from 2017, which shows how much modern compilers optimize and how easy it is to read the assembly they produce. Nicolai Josuttis's initialization talk is a one-hour commitment, so save it for when you have the time. Beyond those, the 2014 talks by Herb Sutter, Mike Acton and Chandler Carruth cover modern style, data-oriented design and data structure performance. Lexical Scanning in Go is an approachable introduction to writing a lexer, even without a parsing background.

programming-language-design.p1: This list is mostly talks that commenters cite to settle arguments that keep coming back. JavaScript: The Good Parts, the 2009 Google TechTalk, is linked on Stack Overflow whenever someone trips over == versus ===, semicolon insertion or prototypes. Armin Ronacher's How Python was Shaped by leaky Internals is the usual reply to why Python is hard to make faster. Maybe Not - Rich Hickey gets sent to anyone debating nulls, Option types or static typing, and Richard Feldman's Why Isn't Functional Programming the Norm? is treated as the stock answer to why some languages win. Alongside these sit lectures and histories people actually finish.
programming-language-design.p2: For a quick first watch, Conway's Game Of Life in APL is short and shows why array languages strike people the way they do. The longer commitment is Lecture 1A of MIT 6.001 Structure and Interpretation from 1986, the opening of a full course, or the Crockford on JavaScript series. Elsewhere you'll find Guy Steele's Growing a Language, Jonathan Blow's 2014 ideas for a games language, C++ initialization pitfalls from CppCon 2018, and Brian Goetz on stewarding Java.

software-performance.p1: This list is mostly conference talks that commenters link as answers to questions that keep coming back. When someone on Stack Overflow is confused about why a promise resolves before a setTimeout callback, the reply is usually Jake Archibald on the web browser event loop, setTimeout, micro tasks, requestAnimationFrame, which leads the list by a wide margin. When a microbenchmark gets optimized away, people point to CppCon 2015: Chandler Carruth "Tuning C++: Benchmarks, and CPUs, and Compilers! Oh My!". Questions about cache behaviour and memory layout get CppCon 2014: Mike Acton "Data-Oriented Design and C++", and the recurring Hacker News question of why Python is hard to speed up gets Armin Ronacher's talk on leaky internals.
software-performance.p2: A good first watch is the Jake Archibald talk from 2018, since it answers one concrete question cleanly and is useful to anyone who writes for the browser. After that, "Performance Matters" by Emery Berger (2019) explains why benchmarks shift after tiny edits and introduces causal profiling. The heavier commitment is the C++ material: Herb Sutter's two-part atomic Weapons and his lock-free programming talks, plus Carruth on containers and Matt Kulukundis on building a cache-friendly hash table. Older picks include a 2009 Google talk on JavaScript speed and a GNU Parallel intro.

satire-parody.p1: This is mostly technical comedy, the kind of thing that gets linked when a thread turns to floating point, conference talks, or a programming language nobody uses yet. The USENIX Security '18-Q: Why Do Keynote Speakers Keep Suggesting That Improving Security Is Possible? is the most rewatched, a funny and sobering take on machine learning and tech hubris. On The Turing Completeness of PowerPoint (SIGBOVIK) comes up whenever absurd computation does, and The Loving Trap is posted as the standard companion to any Adam Curtis film. These are less answers to a question than talks people cite as shorthand, often with a real point underneath the joke.
satire-parody.p2: Start with Chicken chicken chicken from 2007, a short academic talk that commenters treat as required viewing on what not to do at a podium. How to sound smart in your TEDx Talk is a similar quick watch. The bigger commitment is suckerpinch, whose 30 Weird Chess Algorithms: Elo World and NaN Gates and Flip FLOPS reward full attention. Beyond those, the list runs through Erlang The Movie II: The Sequel, Keynes versus Hayek rap battles, A Capella Science parodies, and Onion spoofs.

film-tv-clips.p1: Despite the broad label, this list leans heavily toward science fiction, and most of its links come from Science Fiction & Fantasy Stack Exchange rather than Hacker News. People post these clips as evidence when answering questions. Star Wars Featurette: The Birth of the Lightsaber is cited as a primary source from Lucas and Hamill on how the effects and choreography were made. Origin of the Borg backs up answers about the Collective's history. terminator 2 deleted scenes supplies lore found only in cut footage, such as the T-800's learning-mode chip. Other links answer a recurring request to identify half-remembered 80s and 90s shows and cartoons.
film-tv-clips.p2: For a quick first watch, try Star Wars Origins: The Dam Busters - Side by Side Scene Comparison, which shows how a 1955 war film shaped the Death Star trench run. The long commitment is the full 1988 Earth Star Voyager, a TV movie about cadets on a spaceship that answerers link when someone half-remembers it. The rest of the list runs through Doctor Who, including the 2007 Time Crash special, Star Trek II battle scenes, cartoon intros, and fan commentary on the Star Wars prequels.

compilers-interpreters.p1: This list collects 149 talks about what happens between source code and a running program: lexers, compiler optimizations, linking, coroutine machinery, and the occasional language built for fun. Most recommendations answer a recurring question. Stack Overflow users post Matt Godbolt's CppCon 2017 talk on what the compiler has done for you whenever someone asks what their code turns into, and KotlinConf 2017 - Deep Dive into Coroutines on JVM by Roman Elizarov when suspend functions come up. Others are talks Hacker News simply keeps citing, such as Lexical Scanning in Go - Rob Pike and Clasp: Common Lisp using LLVM and C++ for Molecular Metaprogramming.
compilers-interpreters.p2: Start with Rob Pike's 2011 lexer talk, which commenters describe as easy to follow even without a parsing background. William Byrd's 2017 Papers We Love talk on the most beautiful program ever written asks more of you, deriving the essence of Lisp and moving into program synthesis. The rest leans heavily on C++, including Godbolt's 2018 follow-up on how a program reaches main() and Chandler Carruth on undefined behavior, with side trips into Svelte's reactivity, Java lambdas, and the MoVfuscator.

standup-sketch-comedy.p1: Very little here is comedy in the club or special sense. Most of these videos are funny bits that commenters reach for to make a point in an unrelated argument. George Carlin Talks About "Stuff" turns up in threads on clutter, storage units and consumerism. Patrick Stewart interview - Parkinson - BBC gets linked to people worried about losing their hair. Harder Drive: Hard drives we didn't want or need is cited as silly but genuinely educational computer science. Musicians on Stack Exchange answer questions about the I-V-vi-IV progression with 4 Chords | Music Videos | The Axis Of Awesome. These are apt references, not a curated comedy canon.
standup-sketch-comedy.p2: For a quick first watch, start with one of the Axis of Awesome four chord videos or It's Not About The Nail from 2013, both short and self-contained. Harder Drive, from 2022 and the most recommended entry, is the longer commitment and rewards attention to the technical detail. Jackie Chan - How to Do Action Comedy sits between them as film analysis. The rest runs through Carlin, John Cleese, a Harald Eia TEDx talk on welfare states and social mobility, Captain Disillusion at the Blender Conference, and the Pachelbel Rant.

music-performance.p1: This is less a playlist of favourite songs than a set of videos people link to make a point. The most recommended, Video explains the world's most important 6-sec drum loop, resurfaces on Hacker News whenever sampling, copyright or music history comes up. Fear the Boom and Bust gets passed around as a funny primer on Keynes versus Hayek. Much of the rest comes from Music Stack Exchange answers to recurring questions: 4 Chords | Music Videos | The Axis Of Awesome for the I-V-vi-IV progression, and Carl Verheyen: Whammy Bar Setup Secrets for a Strat tremolo that won't stay in tune.
music-performance.p2: Start with the drum loop video from 2006. It is the one commenters most often call a must-watch, and it sets up why a few seconds of audio matter. Speaking Piano and Adriano Celentano - Prisencolinensinainciusol make good short follow-ups. The long commitment is The Caretaker - Everywhere At The End Of Time - Stages 1-6 (Complete), uploaded in 2019 with all six stages. The rest leans practical: microtonal guitar frets, hand stretches, Bootsy's funk formula, and Benjamin Zander's TED talk on phrasing.

arts-entertainment-other.p1: This is a grab bag, and most of it exists because someone on Science Fiction & Fantasy Stack Exchange was trying to name a show they half remember. Earth Star Voyager (1988), Magi-Nation Season 1 Episode 1 - Final Dreamer and Huntik Secrets Seekers Episode 1 A Seeker Is Born are answers to identification questions about teens on spaceships or kids summoning monsters, and The Price of Life (1987) turns up whenever someone recalls a time-as-money film that predates In Time. The Hacker News picks are different: Joe Ades, Greatest Salesman in New York City History gets cited as a lesson in live selling, and Bryan Cranston's Advice to Aspiring Actors gets applied to job interviews.
arts-entertainment-other.p2: For a quick first watch, start with Bryan Cranston's Advice to Aspiring Actors or the Patrick Stewart interview from Parkinson, which hair-loss threads recommend as a funny take on accepting baldness. The Joe Ades clip from 2008 is the one HN returns to most. The long commitment is Earth Star Voyager, a full 1988 movie. The rest is mostly 80s and 90s intros and pilots, including Captain Power and the Soldiers of the Future, plus the Game of Thrones opening credits and a Doctor Who mini episode.

music-theory-production.p1: This is mostly music explained to people who think about systems. The most cited is Adam Neely's Music Theory and White Supremacy, which commenters reach for when someone treats Western functional harmony as universal, with the raga example doing much of the work. Tantacrul's two essays, Music Software & Bad Interface Design: Avid's Sibelius and Notation Must Die: The Battle For How We Read Music, come up whenever software UX or reinventing notation is debated. Ahoy's Trackers: The Sound of 16-Bit appears in Amiga and demoscene threads. Alongside these sit practical answers from Stack Exchange, such as a recipe for running JACK and PulseAudio together on Linux.
music-theory-production.p2: The quick first watch is The Axis of Awesome's 4 Chords, a comedy demonstration of how many pop songs share I-V-vi-IV, which answerers use whenever common progressions come up. The bigger commitment is the Tantacrul pair, which reward watching together, with Notation Must Die from 2023 being the more recent and fuller argument. The rest spans synthesis basics from matrixsynth, Rick Beato on why adults can't develop perfect pitch, a 2010 adjustable microtonal guitar for makam music, a Clojure talk on functional composition, and GDC's DOOM: Behind the Music.

documentaries-storytelling.p1: This is a list of long-form documentaries and essay films that Hacker News commenters bring up again and again when a thread touches their subject. The Century of the Self (Full Adam Curtis Documentary) gets posted whenever advertising, propaganda or consumer psychology comes up. Video explains the world's most important 6-sec drum loop returns in every argument about sampling and copyright. The first episode of James Burke's Connections is the standard reply to blackouts and supply chain failures. AlphaGo - The Movie is recommended as a human story about AI that non-technical viewers can follow. These are answers people give to recurring conversations, not passing links.
documentaries-storytelling.p2: For a short first watch, try the drum loop video from 2006 or Powers of Ten™ (1977), the Eames film about scale. The longer commitments are the full Adam Curtis series and Stewart Brand's six-part How Buildings Learn. Dick Proenneke in Alone in the Wilderness is a quieter evening, recommended for its picture of self-reliance and handcraft. The rest runs from Fall of Civilizations on the Sumerians to a 2014 Star Wars featurette that Stack Exchange answerers cite on how lightsabers were made.

functional-programming.p1: This list is mostly conference talks and a few university lectures that Hacker News commenters cite when arguments about functional programming come up. Rich Hickey dominates: Simple Made Easy is treated as the standard talk on software complexity and gets recommended to programmers in any language, while The Value of Values with Rich Hickey is the one people credit with convincing them of immutability. Brian Beckman: Don't fear the Monad is the usual answer when someone asks for a monad explanation that actually lands, and The Soul of Erlang and Elixir by Sasa Juric is the standard pitch for the BEAM. These are talks people cite to settle questions, not passing links.
functional-programming.p2: For a quick first watch, Conway's Game Of Life in APL is what commenters share as the fastest way to see why array languages startle people. Jim Weirich's Y Not talk from Ruby Conf 12 is the most recommended overall and makes the Y combinator click even for non-Rubyists. The long commitment is the 1986 MIT 6.001 Structure and Interpretation series, starting with Lecture 1A. The rest covers Elm-style data modeling from Richard Feldman, Clojure practice, and Lisp interpreters.

visual-arts.p1: This is less an art list than a set of talks and process videos that programmers keep handing each other. The most cited is 8 Bit & '8 Bitish' Graphics-Outside the Box, a 2017 GDC talk by an artist behind Loom and Monkey Island on limited palettes and palette cycling. Close behind is Stewart Brand's How Buildings Learn, which commenters read as a lesson in software maintenance, and Christopher Alexander - Patterns in Architecture, cited as the source on Alexander's own doubts about patterns. Photography Stack Exchange answerers add Inside a Camera at 10,000fps - The Slow Mo Guys to settle recurring questions about shutters and flash sync.
visual-arts.p2: For a quick first watch, try !!Con 2017: HDR Photography in Microsoft Excel?! by Kevin Chen, a short talk that explains HDR through a deliberately absurd implementation. The long commitment is Marc Levoy's Lectures on Digital Photography from 2016, a free university course on computational photography. Between those sit David Bull's The Great Wave woodblock process series, Andrea Dorfman's 2010 short How To Be Alone, a Francis Bacon documentary, lens explainers like the crop factor video, and a few pieces on cities and telescopes.

security-hacking.p1: This list splits into two kinds of recommendation. Much of it is reference material that Stack Overflow answerers link when the same questions come up again: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (in plain English) for why the authorization code goes over the back channel, The key to Firebase security - Google I/O 2016 for rules and exposed config keys, and short explainers on prepared statements and password storage. The rest are conference talks Hacker News cites by name, such as Behind the Scenes of iOS Security from Black Hat 2016, Moxie Marlinspike's DEF CON talks on SSL, and 28c3: The Science of Insecurity.
security-hacking.p2: For a quick first watch, try Why Electronic Voting Is Still A Bad Idea, Tom Scott's 2019 case for a general audience, or Computerphile's short 2013 primer on how not to store passwords. The bigger commitment is the talk material. Behind the Scenes of iOS Security is the one HN calls the deepest public look at Apple's keychain and cloud design, and the 2010 and 2011 SSL talks still frame the authenticity debate. Beyond those, the list covers token storage in SPAs, SQL injection and Firestore rules.

cloud-devops-sre.p1: This list splits into two kinds of recommendation. Most of it is Stack Overflow answer material: AWS re:Invent 2018: Amazon DynamoDB Deep Dive: Advanced Design Patterns for DynamoDB (DAT401) gets linked whenever someone asks about single-table design, GSIs or composite keys, and the Firebase Firecasts on Cloud Functions show up when a function hangs or times out because a promise was never returned. The other kind is the talk Hacker News cites in outage threads, such as Richard Cook's Velocity NY 2013 talk on resilience in complex adaptive systems and Bryan Cantrill's Debugging Under Fire, a postmortem people call both funny and instructive.
cloud-devops-sre.p2: If you want something quick and self-contained, start with Cook's 2013 talk, which commenters treat as the clearest account of normalization of deviance and how systems drift toward failure. Then watch Cantrill's 2017 GOTO talk. The bigger commitment is the DynamoDB set from 2018 and 2019, which works best watched together: data modeling first, then the internals talk on replication and consistency. The rest covers containers built from scratch, literate devops in Emacs, AWS networking and Firebase setup and pricing.

privacy-surveillance.p1: This list is mostly conference talks and explainers that commenters link when the same arguments come back around. America Keeps Rejecting an ID Card It Already Has shows up in nearly every identity theft and data breach thread as the short case against SSNs as identifiers. This Video Is Sponsored By ███ VPN is the standard reply to VPN marketing. Moxie Marlinspike's Defcon 18 talk on changing threats to privacy gets cited to answer the just-don't-use-Facebook argument, and The Grugq's OPSEC: Because Jail is for wuftpd is the go-to talk on pseudonymity in threads about Tor and Silk Road. These are rebuttals and reference points more than entertainment.
privacy-surveillance.p2: Start with the CGP Grey video from 2017 or the Tom Scott VPN piece from 2019, both quick and easy to follow. The Last Week Tonight segments on data brokers, government surveillance and pig butchering scams are similarly accessible. The longer commitments are the conference talks: The Grugq and Zoz on why OPSEC is hard, Dan Geer's Cybersecurity as Realpolitik from Black Hat 2014, and Cory Doctorow's talks on the war on general-purpose computing. Frank Abagnale's Talks at Google session rounds it out with practical fraud lessons.

cryptography.p1: This list is mostly made of explainers and conference talks that commenters link when the same questions come up again. The newcomer questions are how Bitcoin works, how two parties agree on a key in public, and why passwords should never be stored in plain text. For those, people reach for But how does bitcoin actually work?, Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange, and How NOT to Store Passwords! - Computerphile, often in Stack Overflow answers as well as Hacker News threads. Alongside them sit talks people cite as primary sources, such as BlackHat USA 2011: SSL And The Future Of Authenticity on the broken certificate authority system, plus a strong skeptical streak on e-voting, blockchains and NFTs.
cryptography.p2: Start with Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange from 2012, a short piece whose paint analogy needs no prior background. Then watch the 3Blue1Brown Bitcoin video from 2017. The longer commitments are the conference talks: Behind the Scenes of iOS Security from Black Hat 2016 and DEFCON 17: More Tricks For Defeating SSL, which covers sslstrip and null-prefix certificates. The rest covers Tom Scott and Computerphile on electronic voting, James Mickens on blockchains, and Folding Ideas on NFTs and Decentraland.

distributed-systems.p1: This list is mostly conference talks that commenters cite when explaining how real systems hold together across machines. Some are pitches that changed minds: The Soul of Erlang and Elixir • Sasa Juric • GOTO 2019 is the talk Hacker News credits with converting people to the BEAM, and Erlang Factory 2014 - That's 'Billion' with a 'B': Scaling to the Next Level at WhatsApp shows a tiny team running a huge messaging service. Others are reference answers. Stack Overflow users link Google I/O 2012 - Go Concurrency Patterns for goroutine questions and the DynamoDB Under the Hood talk from AWS re:Invent 2018 for consistency and replication questions.
distributed-systems.p2: A good first watch is Testing Distributed Systems w/ Deterministic Simulation by Will Wilson from Strange Loop 2014, which commenters treat as the definitive case for simulation testing. Follow it with Martin Kleppmann's Turning the database inside out with Apache Samza, the talk people say reframed caching and event sourcing for them. The long commitment is the 32-hour freeCodeCamp course on Blockchain, Solidity, and Full Stack Web3 Development. The rest runs from Rich Hickey on system design to Firebase, App Engine internals and how Bitcoin works.

university-lectures.p1: This list is mostly full university lectures that commenters keep handing to each other as answers to questions that come up over and over. Someone asks how to give a better talk and gets How to Speak from MIT OpenCourseWare. Someone wants to write more clearly and is sent to LEADERSHIP LAB: The Craft of Writing Effectively. Threads on fusion announcements turn up MIT's Pathway to Fusion Energy (IAP 2017) - Zach Hartwig, and Stats Stack Exchange users link 16. Learning: Support Vector Machines when the math behind support vectors needs explaining. Alongside these single talks sit series people actually finish, such as Sapolsky's 1. Introduction to Human Behavioral Biology.
university-lectures.p2: For a first evening, How to Speak or the UChicago writing lecture are self-contained and immediately useful outside any classroom. The long commitment is Sapolsky's Stanford course from 2011, which commenters describe as funny and eye-opening across many scales of human behavior, or the 1986 MIT 6.001 Structure and Interpretation lectures, where programming often clicks for people. Beyond those, the list covers David Silver's reinforcement learning course, Eric Mazur on why lectures fail, Sapolsky on depression, and Harvard's Justice series.

science-method-communication.p1: This list is mostly old lectures and interview clips that commenters reach for when a thread needs an explanation rather than an argument. Physics Stack Exchange answerers link Richard Feynman. Why. whenever someone asks why a force works, because the honest answer is that physics describes behaviour without a deeper mechanism. The Quantum Conspiracy: What Popularizers of QM Don't Want You to Know, a 2011 Google TechTalk, gets recommended as the talk that made quantum mechanics click for programmers. Is Most Published Research Wrong? shows up whenever a shaky study or p<0.05 comes up, and Hamming, "You and Your Research" is cited as career advice on picking important problems.
science-method-communication.p2: For a quick first watch, start with Richard Feynman Fire, a short clip on fire and photosynthesis that commenters return to as an example of his love of explaining things, then try Powers of Ten™ (1977). The longer commitment is James Burke Connections, Ep. 1 "The Trigger Effect", which opens a full series on how fragile interconnected systems are and resurfaces in every blackout thread. The rest runs from Veritasium pieces on luck and the Higgs boson to worldbuilding notes on sky and plant colour.

operating-systems.p1: This is mostly a list of talks people cite in arguments and oral history people pass around, with a few practical answers mixed in. The Tragedy of systemd is the most-linked item, offered as a balanced BSD-side view whenever the systemd debate flares up. VCF East: Ken Thompson interviewed by Brian Kernighan and AT&T Archives: The UNIX Operating System supply first-hand Unix history and a clear account of pipes from the people who built them. The Thirty Million Line Problem and the 2021 USENIX keynote on operating systems rediscovering hardware get recommended as arguments about complexity and how little the OS really controls.
operating-systems.p2: For a first watch, the 2012 AT&T Unix film is short and clear, and the Thompson interview from 2019 is an easy, funny follow-up. The Thirty Million Line Problem is the long commitment, recommended despite its length. Beyond those, the list covers Matt Godbolt's CppCon 2018 talk on how a program reaches main(), Bryan Cantrill on illumos, jails and Solaris Zones, Liz Rice building containers from scratch, Dalvik internals, TempleOS, and some Ubuntu dual-boot and disk-resizing tutorials from Ask Ubuntu.

philosophy-ethics.p1: This is less a philosophy syllabus than a set of videos people reach for when a thread turns to a question that won't settle. Dominion (2018) - full documentary [Official] gets posted, often forcefully, whenever factory farming comes up, and some commenters say it changed how they eat. We Were Taught to Call Death a Blessing shows up in longevity threads as a compact case for fighting aging. Music and Life - Alan Watts is the reply to posts about burnout and career anxiety. Justice: What's The Right Thing To Do? is the lecture series people actually finish, praised for Michael Sandel's teaching and for giving viewers a vocabulary for ethical arguments.
philosophy-ethics.p2: For a quick first watch, start with The Egg - A Short Story or Optimistic Nihilism, both short Kurzgesagt animations, or the Feynman clip on magnets, which Physics Stack Exchange users link to show where explanations run out. The long commitments are Sandel's Harvard lectures from 2009, the full Dominion documentary, and John Vervaeke's Awakening from the Meaning Crisis series. Around those sit Alain de Botton on status anxiety, the Chomsky and Foucault debate on human nature, an illustrated anarcho-capitalist summary, and a talk on the Mandukya Upanishad.

futurism-technology-society.p1: This is a mixed shelf of talks, essays and explainers that Hacker News and Stack Exchange commenters reach for when a thread turns to where technology is taking us. Some are arguments people cite by name: We Were Taught to Call Death a Blessing turns up in longevity threads as a compact case for fighting aging, Preventing the Collapse of Civilization / Jonathan Blow (Thekla, Inc) is the standard link on software decay and lost knowledge, and Blockchains Are a Bad Idea (James Mickens) is the usual reply in crypto debates. Others are answers to recurring questions, like Isaac Arthur's Starlifting, which Worldbuilding answerers post whenever someone wants to pull mass off a star.
futurism-technology-society.p2: The CGP Grey video on death is the quick first watch, short and easy to pass along. The longer commitments are the lectures: Joseph Tainter on the collapse of complex societies, Neil Postman on the surrender of culture to technology from 2013, and Peter Thiel's 2019 conversation on stagnation with Eric Weinstein. Between those sit critiques of ad-driven platforms, such as Zeynep Tufekci's 2017 TED talk, and a long run of Isaac Arthur megastructure episodes like Dyson Spheres and Shellworlds.

systems-other.p1: This is a grab bag, and most of it comes from Stack Exchange answer threads rather than Hacker News debates. The most linked item, Tutorial: Android Internals -  Building a Custom ROM, Pt. 1 of 2, is the standard pointer when someone asks how to build firmware from AOSP source. Bitcoin 101 - Quindecillions & The Amazing Math Of Bitcoin's Private Keys gets cited to explain why brute-forcing keys is not a real threat. Fix-it clips like the Windows MBR partition table error answer recurring questions. Hacker News contributes mainly one cited talk, James Hamilton's Velocity 2010 datacenter cost breakdown.
systems-other.p2: For a quick first watch, try What is Bitcoin Mining?, which answerers offer as a friendly starting point, or the private keys video if you want the math of key space. The heavier commitments are the 2011 Android ROM tutorial, the first of two parts, and the conference recordings, especially Scaling Bitcoin 2016 Milan, a full morning session. The rest is practical troubleshooting: Windows Server FTP setup, VMware conflicts with Device Guard, an Ubuntu login loop, plus an IPv6 adoption talk from Wells Fargo.

productivity-self-improvement.p1: This is the shelf of talks Hacker News sends people to when the conversation turns to how to work, study, speak or decide what to do with a career. Some are answers to recurring questions: How to Speak from MIT OpenCourseWare is the default reply whenever someone asks how to give a presentation, and Mike Monteiro: F*ck You, Pay Me comes up every time a freelancer has a client who won't pay. Others are talks people quote from memory, like Steve Jobs Stanford Commencement Speech 2005 and Randy Pausch's Last Lecture: Achieving Your Childhood Dreams, passed to graduates and anyone at a crossroads.
productivity-self-improvement.p2: A quick first watch is the Jobs commencement address, about fifteen minutes, or one of the short CGP Grey videos such as You Need a Theme, Not a Goal from 2020. The larger commitments are How to Speak and the Pausch lecture from 2007, each well over an hour. The rest covers focus and study habits through Marty Lobdell - Study Less Study Smart and Huberman on dopamine, thinking before coding in Hammock Driven Development, and Hamming's 1995 talk You and Your Research.

ideas-education-other.p1: This is a grab bag of talks that tend to surface when a thread drifts toward how people learn, choose and work together. Many are TED talks from 2007 to 2011 that commenters cite as shorthand for an argument: The paradox of choice for why too many options lead to paralysis, Do schools kill creativity? in schooling debates (though some dispute its conclusions), and Massive-scale online collaboration as the inventor's own account of human computation. Others answer a recurring practical question, like Your Post Code Is the Directions, Not the Destination whenever addresses or geospatial data come up, or Designing Earth-like Atmospheres for worldbuilders sizing up invented planets.
ideas-education-other.p2: The quick first watch is How to tie your shoes, a small fix many commenters say they adopted for good. From there, Learning from dirty jobs suits anyone weighing trades or the follow-your-passion advice, and Social Physics: How Good Ideas Spread, a 2014 Talks at Google session, is the more substantial sit-down, on how connectivity drives productivity. The rest covers simpler living, the call to learn, indoor air, and two CGP Grey explainers, one from 2011 on daylight saving and one from 2025 on post codes.

religion-belief.p1: This list is less about arguing for or against God than about how people come to believe things. The most recommended item, In Search Of A Flat Earth by Folding Ideas, is treated on Hacker News as the definitive and compassionate account of why people fall into conspiracy theories, and it sits alongside Mick West's UFO breakdowns and Miniminuteman's reply to Ancient Apocalypse. Other picks are talks people cite in arguments, like the Krauss lecture A Universe From Nothing or John Oliver on televangelists, while Stack Exchange users link Swami Sarvapriyananda and Yuttadhammo Bhikkhu as direct answers to recurring questions about the Upanishads, lust and addiction.
religion-belief.p2: For a quick first watch, try Televangelists: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver, the go-to explainer on seed faith fundraising, or Gimbal UFO - A New Analysis from 2022. The long commitment is Jordan Peterson's 2017 Maps of Meaning series, which several commenters say they worked through during depression. Between those, Irving Finkel's talk on cuneiform tablets and ESOTERICA's history of Yahweh cover the ancient roots of religion, and Hans Rosling's Religions and babies brings in population data.

transit-urbanism.p1: This corner of the list is dominated by one channel, Not Just Bikes, whose videos have become the stock replies in Hacker News threads about cars, cities and housing. When someone argues that snow makes cycling impossible, commenters post Why Canadians Can't Bike in the Winter (but Finnish people can). When a thread turns to municipal budgets, Why American Cities Are Broke - The Growth Ponzi Scheme [ST03] appears as the clearest account of how low-density infrastructure is financed. Stroads are Ugly, Expensive, and Dangerous (and they're everywhere) [ST05] serves as the standard introduction to car-centric road design. These are answers to recurring arguments more than lectures, and each settles a specific point.
transit-urbanism.p2: A reasonable first watch is Why This Channel Exists (and why I hate Houston), from 2021, which commenters treat as the entry point to the whole argument about North American car dependency. The longer commitment is How Self-Driving Cars will Destroy Cities (and what to do about it), a 2024 video essay that shows up in nearly every Waymo thread as the main counterargument. Beyond those, the list covers speed limits, traffic noise, Dutch cycle paths as documented by BicycleDutch in 2011, Japanese zoning, and an LED traffic light piece from Technology Connections.

aviation.p1: This is mostly a list of answers to recurring questions. On Aviation Stack Exchange, people asking how lift really works get sent to how wings work? Smoke streamlines around an airfoil for the picture and to Doug McLean | Common Misconceptions in Aerodynamics for the physics, while questions about heavy maintenance get British Airways Boeing 747-400 in D-Check. Hacker News uses the list differently, as a set of talks it cites in arguments. Children Of The Magenta Line, recommended in twelve separate comments, comes up whenever autopilot, Tesla FSD or self-driving crashes are discussed, as the standard lecture on what automation dependency does to pilots.
aviation.p2: For a quick first watch, try Why You Should Put YOUR MASK On First (My Brain Without Oxygen) - Smarter Every Day 157, a 2016 demonstration of hypoxia quietly wrecking judgment. The longer commitment is the Lex Fridman Podcast #122 conversation with David Fravor from 2020, a full podcast episode. Around those sit explainers on airline economics and boarding from Wendover Productions and CGP Grey, Real Engineering on Zipline's drone deliveries in Rwanda, Scott Manley on heat shields, and engineering history such as The Mighty J58 and the Makani kite energy film.

language-linguistics.p1: This is less a linguistics syllabus than a pile of things people reach for when a language argument breaks out. Stephen Fry Kinetic Typography - Language gets posted whenever a thread turns into grammar policing, as the short case for language change. What Languages Sound Like To Foreigners and Adriano Celentano - Prisencolinensinainciusol surface whenever fake languages and accents come up, as examples of gibberish that sounds real. George Lakoff: Moral Politics is the talk people say changed how they hear political speech. On English Stack Exchange, Dr Geoff Lindsey's Why these English phonetic symbols are all WRONG works as a standing answer to questions about vowels and syllables.
language-linguistics.p2: Start with the Sara Forsberg video from 2014 or the Celentano song, both quick and the most widely shared here. The Fry piece from 2010 is similarly short. For a long commitment, Leonard Bernstein's 1973 Norton lectures on musical phonology and Borges's This Craft of Verse lectures run as series. In between are Irving Finkel's two talks on cuneiform and the ancient world, Lindsey's phonetics explainers, a CGP Grey video on US tribes, and George Carlin on euphemisms.

manufacturing-industry.p1: This list is mostly factory tours, process explainers and a few investigations, and Hacker News commenters reach for them when a thread turns to how physical things get made. The Ingenious Design of the Aluminum Beverage Can comes up whenever cans or mass-produced objects are mentioned. Origins of Precision gets cited in machining and chip threads for how precision is bootstrapped from nothing. I Tried To Make Something In America (The Smarter Scrubber Experiment) - Smarter Every Day 308 has become a standard reference in arguments about lost US manufacturing, and The Boeing 787: Broken Dreams l Al Jazeera Investigations is cited as early evidence of Boeing's quality problems, years before the 737 MAX.
manufacturing-industry.p2: Start with the beverage can video, a short engineerguy piece from 2015 that shows the style of the better entries. Origins of Precision is the longer sit-down, about half an hour. From there the list splits between tours, such as the ULA rocket factory and Inside a Huge PCB Factory, craft pieces like The Art of Making a Nixie Tube, and industry context like the WIRED Shenzhen documentary and Branch Education's 2025 explainer on EUV photolithography. EEVblog's 2010 DFM tutorial is for anyone taking a board to production.

home-diy-repair.p1: This is mostly a shelf of answers to recurring practical questions, with a few explainers that Hacker News treats as required viewing. The most cited is Technology Connections' Detergent packs are kinda wishy-washy (Dishwashers Explained), linked whenever dishwashers or pods come up, along with its follow-up I messed up. You're using too much detergent. DIY Perks' Building a realistic artificial sun (for dark winter days) surfaces in threads on seasonal affective disorder and bright home lighting. The rest comes largely from Stack Exchange answerers, who link Park Tool's How to Adjust a Front Derailleur as the standard fix for dropped chains and rubbing.
home-diy-repair.p2: Start with How to Adjust a Front Derailleur or the 2017 rear derailleur video from Park Tool, which are focused repair walk-throughs you can follow with a bike on the stand. The long commitment is the 2020 dishwasher video, which runs over 30 minutes but changes how people load and dose their machines. Beyond that, the list covers hydraulic brake pistons, headlight restoration, a MacBook Pro drive cable fix, connecting two routers over Ethernet, and Windows chores like setting environment variables.

engineering-making-other.p1: This is the drawer where Hacker News keeps its answers to recurring arguments about everyday objects. When someone repeats the claim that bulbs were made to fail, Longer-lasting light bulbs: it was complicated gets linked as the engineer's account of the lifespan versus efficiency tradeoff. When plugs come up, British Plugs Are Better Than All Other Plugs, And Here's Why follows for its safety reasoning. Your dishwasher is better than you think (tips, tricks, and how they work) is the guide people send to friends, and Old car headlights were all the same , which was a fairly bright idea serves as a case study in mandating requirements rather than solutions.
engineering-making-other.p2: Tom Scott's 2014 plug video is the quick first watch and explains why it gets posted so reliably. The long commitment is Construction of the 10000 year clock - Alexander Rose (SETI Talks), a 2011 talk commenters admit is long but cite in threads about structures and knowledge meant to outlast generations. Beyond those, the list runs through Tim Hunkin's vacuum cleaner episode, Mark Rober's porch pirate glitter bomb, the Miniatur Wunderland model railway, and a cluster on product safety, from a dangerous USB charger to fake fuses sold on Amazon.

civil-engineering-construction.p1: This is less a civil engineering syllabus than a set of videos people reach for when an infrastructure argument starts. The most cited is Stroads are Ugly, Expensive, and Dangerous (and they're everywhere) [ST05], which Hacker News treats as the standard introduction to car-centric road design. What Really Happened During the Texas Power Grid Outage? gets linked whenever the grid fails, as the calm technical account that cuts through the blame. World's Largest Batteries - (Pumped Storage) settles energy storage threads. Building a Cathedral without Science or Mathematics: The Engineering Method Explained is cited for its argument that engineering is rule-of-thumb problem solving older than formal science.
civil-engineering-construction.p2: A good first watch is Tom Scott's Why Do Reversing Trucks Not Beep Any More? from 2014, or the 2008 clip of the Taipei 101 damper moving during an earthquake. The long commitment is Stewart Brand's How Buildings Learn, a six-part series from 2012 that software people value for its view of buildings as systems that change with maintenance. Beyond that, the list runs from Isaac Arthur's speculative Orbital Rings and Arcologies to Patrick Boyle's skeptical 2024 look at Neom and Wendover's piece on Chinese railways.

tech-company-stories.p1: This list is mostly the films and talks that Hacker News reaches for when a thread turns to how a tech company was built or how it fell apart. Micro Men is the most recommended, a dramatization of Sinclair versus Acorn that commenters bring up whenever ARM's origins come up. Project Code Rush follows Netscape engineers through the open-sourcing of Mozilla in the late 90s. Ed Catmull, Pixar: Keep Your Crises Small gets cited as advice on running creative teams, and LISA11 - Fork Yeah! The Rise and Development of illumos is the account people link, along with its line about Ellison and the lawnmower, whenever Oracle behaves badly.
tech-company-stories.p2: For a quick first watch, try Steve Jobs Insult Response or the Catmull talk, both of which are short enough to finish before deciding on more. The long commitment is the iPhone 1 keynote from MacWorld 2007, which runs 80 minutes, or The Spectacular Failure of the Star Wars Hotel from 2024, which commenters say holds up despite its length. Beyond those, the list covers the military roots of Silicon Valley, Valve's Half-Life 2 retrospective, Disney's FastPass, and Facebook ad fraud.

history-of-computing.p1: This is a list of 242 videos on computing history. It mixes archival films, interviews, dramatizations, and talks by people who built the field. Hacker News commenters share these mostly as talks they cite and films they rewatch. AT&T Archives: The UNIX Operating System and VCF East: Ken Thompson interviewed by Brian Kernighan come up whenever Unix origins are discussed, and the Thompson interview is valued for stories even Kernighan had not heard. Micro Men - 720p (2009) is the usual answer to how Sinclair and Acorn led to ARM. Alan Kay - Normal Considered Harmful turns up on must-watch lists as an argument against ahistorical software.
history-of-computing.p2: For a quick first watch, start with The Mother of All Demos, presented by Douglas Engelbart (1968), or the Kernighan interview from 2019. The longer commitment is Mechanical Computer (All Parts) - Basic Mechanisms In Fire Control Computers, a multi-part Navy film that commenters call beautiful and approachable. Beyond those, the list covers the Apollo Guidance Computer from two angles, Netscape in the late 90s, Alan Kay and Ted Nelson, and an AT&T film on wave behavior.

cooking-food.p1: This is mostly a coffee and kitchen-equipment list, with a strong lean toward measurement and myth-checking. Coffee Stack Exchange answerers keep linking The Ultimate French Press Technique as the standard fix for bitter or muddy press coffee, while Hacker News threads on voltage and gas stoves return again and again to Why don't Americans use electric kettles? for its measured comparison. Is olive oil safe at high heat? Does it taste bad? gets cited to settle a stubborn myth with sources and food scientists. These are less lectures than answers to recurring questions, plus a few Technology Connections pieces people share for their engineer's view of ordinary appliances.
cooking-food.p2: For a quick first watch, try Fastest Way To Peel Garlic from Food Wishes (2013), a single trick that Cooking Stack Exchange answerers recommend for peeling garlic in bulk, or Learn Jacques Pépin's famous omelet techniques, two omelet styles in about five minutes. The bigger time investment is the Technology Connections run on drip coffee makers, kettles and an antique microwave. The rest covers moka pot and AeroPress brewing, carbon steel skillets and seasoning, sourdough pizza, deboning a chicken, and why Hershey bars taste the way they do.

gui-hci-history.p1: This is the shelf of talks and demos that Hacker News reaches for whenever a thread turns to why our tools look the way they do. Bret Victor - Inventing on Principle is the standard citation for instant feedback in programming environments, and The Future of Programming is treated as required viewing on how good ideas from the 1960s and 70s were dropped. The Mother of All Demos, presented by Douglas Engelbart (1968) gets posted to show how much was already working that year, while A Tour of the Acme Editor answers the recurring question of what Acme actually is. These are cited talks, offered as evidence in arguments rather than as tutorials.
gui-hci-history.p2: A sensible first watch is Ivan Sutherland Sketchpad Demo 1963 or the Steve Jobs bicycle for our minds clip, both brief and easy context for the rest. Inventing on Principle is the natural second. The longer commitment is Alan Kay, especially Doing with Images Makes Symbols (Full Version) and his OOPSLA 1997 talk, which reward watching in full. Beyond those, the list covers Xerox Cedar, the Symbolics Lisp Machine, Ted Nelson, Eve's In Search of Tomorrow, and a history of the mouse cursor.

hacker-culture-free-software.p1: This is less a tour of free software history than a set of talks Hacker News reaches for when certain arguments come back around. Indistinguishable From Magic: Manufacturing Modern Computer Chips is the most recommended, offered again and again as the best in-depth introduction to how chips are made. 28c3: The coming war on general computation and Cory Doctorow's Civil War General-Purpose Computing talk get cited whenever DRM or locked-down devices come up, often with a note about how prescient they were. Copying Is Not Theft - Official Version is linked in nearly every piracy debate. Most of these are references people cite, not lectures people work through.
hacker-culture-free-software.p2: Copying Is Not Theft is the quick first watch, a short explainer from 2010. The chip manufacturing talk from 2012 is the bigger commitment and the one people most want to see updated. Project Code Rush - The Beginnings of Netscape / Mozilla Documentary makes a good evening on its own. The rest runs from the people side of maintaining open source and Blender's history to elevator hacking at HOPE X, the political history of X, and the future of LaTeX.

computing-history-other.p1: This is the grab bag of computing culture: songs, satire, ads and software curiosities that commenters link when a thread drifts toward nostalgia or a joke needs a punchline. MC Frontalot - It Is Pitch Dark leads the list, surfacing whenever Zork or text adventures come up as a tribute for geeks. Nathan Barley - Episode 1 gets passed around as a savage parody of startup culture that arrived early, and Excel 97 Easter Egg - Flight Simulation is the go-to example of the elaborate hidden games old Office shipped with. Few of these are recommended in earnest. Most are reference points, dropped into a conversation because everyone already half remembers them.
computing-history-other.p2: Start with the Excel 97 flight simulator clip or the Qwest commercial 1999 - Every Movie, both short and both a good measure of how the late nineties imagined its software and its future. The longer commitment is Max Headroom 20 minutes into the future 1985, which commenters call a surprisingly good original film, or the full first episode of Nathan Barley. The rest is quick material: Silicon Valley scenes with Russ Hanneman and Gavin Belson, Don't Copy That Floppy, Clippy, the ICQ sound and Winamp's llama.

social-issues-culture.p1: This is less a syllabus than a set of videos that commenters pull out when a familiar argument starts again. When a thread turns to overpopulation, someone posts DON'T PANIC , Hans Rosling showing the facts about population to show birth rates already falling. Every data breach brings out America Keeps Rejecting an ID Card It Already Has, a short explainer on why Social Security numbers make poor identifiers. Homelessness threads about San Francisco and Seattle cite Seattle is Dying, though some read it as pro-law-enforcement framing. Music Theory and White Supremacy is the most recommended overall, held up as the clearest case that music theory describes one Western tradition rather than music in general.
social-issues-culture.p2: The CGP Grey video from 2017 is the quick first watch and needs no background. The longest commitment is the Marshall Rosenberg nonviolent communication workshop, posted in full with subtitles. Between those, the list covers online culture through ContraPoints on incels and Innuendo Studios on the reaction to Anita Sarkeesian, status through Alain de Botton, the 1965 James Baldwin and William F. Buckley debate, and urban living in Not Just Bikes. Immigration, World Poverty and Gumballs is useful but is plainly advocacy.

media-journalism.p1: This list is less about the news cycle than about how belief and persuasion get manufactured. The most recommended entry, In Search Of A Flat Earth, is what commenters link when someone asks why people fall into conspiracy theories, and it is valued for being compassionate rather than mocking. The Century of the Self (Full Adam Curtis Documentary) shows up in nearly every thread on advertising and propaganda as the origin story of consumer society, usually paired with The Loving Trap, a parody that pokes at Curtis's style and his claims. Others are topical references, such as The Spider's Web: Britain's Second Empire | The Secret World of Finance for tax haven threads.
media-journalism.p2: For a short first watch, start with May 1, 1969: Fred Rogers testifies before the Senate Subcommittee on Communications, a few minutes of persuasive speaking that people cite in public broadcasting debates. The long commitment is The Century of the Self, which runs to several hours across its parts. Folding Ideas fills the middle with Contrepreneurs: The Mikkelsen Twins and Line Goes Up, both from 2022. The rest covers Afghanistan, Sinclair Broadcast Group, fake science publishing, and local news documentaries.

geopolitics-foreign-policy.p1: Most of these 148 videos surface when a news event sends Hacker News looking for background. The Finnish intelligence colonel's talk Tiedustelueverstin arvio Venäjästä | 3.12.2018 spread widely after the 2022 invasion as an explanation of Russian mindset, corruption and propaganda, though some doubt the presenter's rigor. Vladimir Pozner: How the United States Created Vladimir Putin got passed around in the same threads as a non-Western view of Russia-West relations. This Is What Winning Looks Like (Full Length) returned during the Afghanistan withdrawal, and Dr Shashi Tharoor MP - Britain Does Owe Reparations gets linked whenever colonial history comes up. These are mostly talks people cite to settle or deepen an argument.
geopolitics-foreign-policy.p2: For a short first watch, The EU Has Orbits, and the UK Fell Out of All of Them gives a clear picture of the Brexit options, with the caveat that it was made in 2019, before the final outcome. The long commitment is Timothy Snyder's Yale course The Making of Modern Ukraine, which starts with Class 1 and is praised as well taught. The rest covers Cold War subversion interviews with Yuri Bezmenov, disinformation, China's social credit and Covid origins, chip manufacturing as power, and climate geopolitics.

world-history.p1: This list leans heavily on CGP Grey, whose short explainers have become the stock replies to questions that keep coming up in threads. When someone mixes up Britain, the UK and England, a commenter links The UK Is a Country Made of Countries. When finance threads turn to the Square Mile, London Swallowed a City but Couldn't Digest It. appears. Try to Rule Fairly and You'll Be Overthrown is the most cited of all, used as a compact account of political incentives that people apply to companies and workplaces as readily as to governments. Around these sit longer talks and documentaries that commenters cite on debt, empire, offshore finance and Russia.
world-history.p2: Start with Try to Rule Fairly and You'll Be Overthrown, a 2016 video that takes little time and explains why the rest of the list gets quoted so often. The long commitment is 8. The Sumerians - Fall of the First Cities, which commenters describe as audiobook length and recommend as an introduction to early Mesopotamia. After that the list moves between Ray Dalio's 2022 talk on debt and empire cycles, David Graeber on Debt: The First 5,000 Years, The Spider's Web on British tax havens, and a Finnish intelligence colonel's assessment of Russia.

us-politics.p1: Most of what lives here is less about the daily news cycle than about why American politics works the way it does. Hacker News commenters reach for these videos as answers to questions that keep coming back: why the US has two parties, why Congress seems stuck, whether voting machines can be trusted. Why Your Vote Doesn't Count is the standard reply in any first-past-the-post thread, and Why Electronic Voting Is Still A Bad Idea gets linked whenever voting technology comes up. George Lakoff: Moral Politics is cited by people who say it changed how they hear political speech. Antonin Scalia - On American Exceptionalism is offered as a clear case for why gridlock is by design.
us-politics.p2: Start with Why Your Vote Doesn't Count, CGP Grey's short 2011 explainer, then his follow-ups on alternative voting systems. The long commitment is The Cardboard Box Reform - Nixon's Ghost Bill & A Crucial Flaw in Democracy, a long, evidence-backed theory of what changed in Congress in the 1970s. Lawrence Lessig's talks on money in politics and Elizabeth Warren's 2008 lecture on the middle class fill the middle. The rest is historical record: Fred Rogers before the Senate in 1969, James Baldwin debating William F. Buckley in 1965, and Jon Stewart on Crossfire.

military-warfare.p1: This is less a military history syllabus than a set of videos that engineers keep passing around when a war, a weapon or a piece of defense-funded technology comes up in a thread. The most recommended are two uploads of the Navy training film on fire control computers, Mechanical Computer (All Parts) - Basic Mechanisms In Fire Control Computers and the PeriscopeFilm version, which commenters cite as the clearest account of analog mechanical computation, differential gears included. Others surface around news: This Is What Winning Looks Like (Full Length) during the Afghanistan withdrawal, and a Finnish intelligence colonel's talk, Tiedustelueverstin arvio Venäjästä, after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
military-warfare.p2: The quick first watch is one part of the fire control film, which many people say they have rewatched; the 2011 compilation runs all parts together if you want the full course. For a longer evening, The Battle of Midway 1942: Told from the Japanese Perspective is a three-part series built on dense maps and narration about command under uncertainty. The rest covers Secret History of Silicon Valley and its military funding, nuclear weapons explainers, autonomous weapons, Threads, and a cluster of UFO sightings told by a pilot and questioned by Mick West.

ux-ui-design.p1: This list mixes two kinds of recommendation. One is the talk people cite in arguments: Bret Victor - Inventing on Principle comes up in nearly every Hacker News thread on live coding, visual programming or developer tools, and Mike Monteiro: F*ck You, Pay Me gets passed to freelancers whenever unpaid invoices or contracts come up. Tantacrul's Music Software & Bad Interface Design: Avid's Sibelius is the design critique people point to as a crash course in UX mistakes. The other kind is the practical answer on Stack Overflow, where clips like DevBytes: ListView Animations and Learn flexbox the easy way get linked to solve specific layout and animation problems.
ux-ui-design.p2: A good first watch is the Sibelius critique from 2018, which commenters describe as entertaining as well as serious, and it leads naturally into Notation Must Die: The Battle For How We Read Music from 2023, a fuller look at why reinventing notation keeps failing. Inventing on Principle is the one to set aside an evening for. Much of the rest is reference material: Android DevBytes from 2013 on transitions and list animations, iOS 8 constraints and size classes, ConstraintLayout, and CSS flexbox tutorials.

politics-history-other.p1: This corner is dominated by CGP Grey, whose short explainers have become Hacker News's stock answers to questions that come up again and again. Try to Rule Fairly and You'll Be Overthrown is cited as a compact model of how power and incentives work, applied as readily to companies and workplaces as to governments. The UK Is a Country Made of Countries settles the Britain, UK and England confusion, America Keeps Rejecting an ID Card It Already Has turns up in nearly every data breach thread about SSNs, and The Voting System That's Actually Too Good for Politicians to Allow is the default link for STV whenever voting reform or gerrymandering comes up.
politics-history-other.p2: Start with Try to Rule Fairly and You'll Be Overthrown from 2016, the most recommended video here and a quick watch. The longer commitment is the 2013 subtitled debate between Noam Chomsky and Michel Foucault on human nature, which commenters call revealing even if the two mostly talk past each other. Beyond that, the list covers the City of London across two Grey videos, MMP voting, public land in America, Louisiana's poverty, an RSA talk on capitalism, and a 2020 interview arguing against lockdowns.

creative-coding-generative-art.p1: This list collects the talks, demos and coding videos that Hacker News commenters reach for when someone asks how pictures, music or worlds can come out of code. Much of it is cited as proof of what is possible: Elevated by RGBA and TBC appears twice, held up as the benchmark for procedural generation in 4K and as a rebuke to software bloat. Inigo Quilez's Painting a Character with Maths is the usual answer for anyone curious about SDFs. 8 Bit & '8 Bitish' Graphics-Outside the Box, from an artist behind Loom and Monkey Island, gets recommended for its lessons on limited palettes and palette cycling, while The Art of Code - Dylan Beattie is named among the best programming talks.
creative-coding-generative-art.p2: A quick first watch is the 2011 Elevated 4k intro itself, which lets you see the result before reading about how it was made. Painting a Character with Maths and its 2022 follow-up, I painted a Landscape with Mathematics, ask more patience but reward it. Sebastian Lague's Procedural Landmass Generation series from 2016 is the longer commitment. The rest runs from music theory in Functional Composition - Chris Ford to ant and slime simulations, fantasy map tectonics, VR live coding and Darius Kazemi's talk on trying many small things.

free-speech-censorship.p1: This list is mostly what Hacker News reaches for when a thread turns to speech, copyright, surveillance, or money in politics. The most cited is Republic, Lost, Lawrence Lessig's Talks at Google lecture, which commenters post whenever lobbying or SOPA comes up and which several say changed their minds. Christopher Hitchens - Free Speech gets linked in nearly every content moderation argument as the strongest case for open expression. Civil War General-Purpose Computing and 28c3: The coming war on general computation serve as standing references on DRM and locked devices. These are talks people cite to settle recurring arguments, not to break news.
free-speech-censorship.p2: For a quick first watch, Copying Is Not Theft - Official Version is a short explainer from 2010 that makes its point fast. The bigger commitment is Joe Rogan Experience #1258 from 2019, a full podcast conversation with Jack Dorsey, Vijaya Gadde and Tim Pool about how Twitter handled moderation. Between those sit Lessig's 2013 TED talk, the 1965 Baldwin and Buckley debate in two uploads, Jon Haidt on campus values, a 2012 whistleblower panel with Thomas Drake and William Binney, and the Jordan Peterson interview on Channel 4 News.

vr-ar-spatial.p1: Much of this list is John Carmack talking about VR, and Hacker News keeps linking those talks because he explains latency, buffering and comfort as someone who had to solve them. QuakeCon 2012 - John Carmack Keynote is the one cited most, for its VR segment and his views on Linux gaming. Around the Carmack material sit demos people point to when a new idea resurfaces: Head Tracking for Desktop VR Displays using the WiiRemote whenever a 3D display appears, RiftSketch: Live coding in VR with the Oculus Rift, Firefox WebVR, JavaScript and Three.js when programming in VR comes up, and The Future is a Dead Mall - Decentraland and the Metaverse as the standard rebuttal to metaverse claims.
vr-ar-spatial.p2: Start with Johnny Lee's WiiRemote head tracking demo from 2007, a short watch that still explains parallax displays better than most product launches. RiftSketch is similarly quick. The long commitment is the Carmack material: the 2012 QuakeCon keynote, the 2015 Oculus Connect 2 live coding session in Racket, and the 2021 Connect keynote. The Folding Ideas essay runs long too. Elsewhere you get Henry Segerman's non-euclidean VR for hyperbolic space, a Looking Glass monitor teardown, and a couple of more forgiving looks at VRChat and the metaverse.

film-video-production.p1: This list splits into two kinds of video. One half is film analysis that Hacker News commenters pass around whenever a thread turns to how movies work, led by Every Frame a Painting essays like Jackie Chan - How to Do Action Comedy and Akira Kurosawa - Composing Movement, which people cite as unusually well researched explanations of staging and editing. The other half is practical: Blender Stack Exchange answerers link Introduction to Camera Tracking in Blender as the standard walkthrough for putting 3D objects into live footage, and Movies & TV answerers use Bullet Time and The Matrix to explain how camera-array shots are made.
film-video-production.p2: For a quick first watch, Vancouver Never Plays Itself is short and funny, a look at how one city stands in for others on screen. Follow it with the other 2014 and 2015 Every Frame a Painting essays, including Edgar Wright - How to Do Visual Comedy. The long commitment is Mikeycal Meyers' numbered Blender Video Editing series, which runs to at least 24 parts and answers specific questions like laggy previews. The rest covers motion tracking, virtual backlots, and how much CGI hides in so-called practical films.

design-graphics-other.p1: Despite the broad label, this list is almost entirely Blender tutorials, and the recommendations come mostly from Blender Stack Exchange rather than Hacker News. They work as stock answers to recurring questions. Blender Intermediate UV Unwrapping Tutorial gets linked whenever a texture looks stretched or missing because the mesh was never unwrapped properly. How to make Photorealistic Materials in Blender, using the Principled Shader serves as the standard explanation of that node for glass, metals and PBR maps. Introduction to Cycles Baking covers baking setup, and Quick Rigging With Rigify in Blender - Beginner Tutorial walks through generating a rig. A few outliers, such as an Illustrator variable data video, round it out.
design-graphics-other.p2: If you are new to Blender, start with Blender 2.7 Tutorial #0 : Introduction #b3d from BornCG, the entry point of a full basics series and the longest commitment here if you follow it through. Otherwise the UV unwrapping video is the sensible first watch, since so many texture problems trace back to it. The rest is mostly Blender Guru material from 2012 to 2020 on texturing, tiling and city building, plus the Humane Rigging series for anyone fighting armatures and weight painting.

computer-graphics-rendering.p1: This list splits into two camps. On Hacker News, the recurring picks are explainers people cite when graphics and math meet: Freya Holmér's The Beauty of Bézier Curves and its follow-up The Continuity of Splines, Inigo Quilez's Painting a Character with Maths, and minutephysics on Computer Color is Broken. The 4k demo elevated by Rgba & TBC turns up as a landmark and as an argument against software bloat. The larger share comes from Blender Stack Exchange, where tutorials like UV Unwrapping - Blender 2.80 Fundamentals are linked as answers to the same questions about seams, stretched textures and mapping.
computer-graphics-rendering.p2: For a quick first watch, Computer Color is Broken from 2015 is short and changes how you think about blending. Then watch The Beauty of Bézier Curves (2021) and The Continuity of Splines (2022) back to back, since the second builds on the first. Painting a Character with Maths is the heavier commitment. The Blender material, mostly from 2013 to 2019, is reference to consult as needed: texture coordinates, microdisplacement, Cycles baking, Principled Shader materials, Rigify rigging, and ways to speed up renders.

product-industrial-design.p1: This is less a design course than a collection of objects people argue about. The most recommended entry, The Ingenious Design of the Aluminum Beverage Can, shows up whenever cans or mass-produced things come up, and British Plugs Are Better Than All Other Plugs, And Here's Why is the standard reply in any thread about sockets and safety. Steve Jobs Insult Response gets linked as a compact statement of starting from the customer rather than the technology, while Microsoft Re-Designs the iPod Packaging resurfaces every time Microsoft names or markets something confusingly. Most of these work as answers to questions that keep coming back, not as tutorials.
product-industrial-design.p2: The can video from 2015 is the obvious first watch: short, concrete, and the one people most often pass along. Follow it with Steve Jobs Insult Response, then The Grille Trend that Kills 509 People per Year, which commenters use to connect truck front ends to pedestrian deaths. The rest wanders usefully, from Posy's Segmented Displays and The Antique Microwave Oven that's Better than Yours to a TEDx talk on sitting without back pain and a 2008 Nokia concept phone.

everyday-physics-demos.p1: This list is mostly short explainers that commenters link when a recurring question comes up, rather than talks or lecture series. On Physics Stack Exchange, The Biggest Misconception About Electricity is the usual reference in threads about the Poynting vector and the 1/c bulb puzzle. Optics: Destructive interference - Where does the light go? gets cited whenever someone asks where the energy goes. Aviation users link the smoke streamline clip on airfoils to put the equal transit theory to rest. Hacker News readers favor older material too. AT&T Archives: Similiarities of Wave Behavior (Bonus Edition) is repeatedly named the clearest introduction to waves and transmission lines.
everyday-physics-demos.p2: For a quick first watch, try Slow Motion Flipping Cat Physics | Smarter Every Day 58 from 2012. It shows how a body with moving parts can rotate in free fall without external torque. The AT&T wave film rewards a slower, more attentive sitting. Heat Pumps: the Future of Home Heating (2021) is the friendly default on that subject. The remaining 437 videos cover magnets, gravity, relativity, orbital mechanics such as throwing objects from the ISS, and even designing realistic climates.

animation-vfx.p1: Most of the 348 videos here are Blender tutorials that Blender Stack Exchange answerers link when the same questions come up again and again: why textures stretch, why Cycles renders are slow or noisy, how to rig a character. UV Unwrapping - Blender 2.80 Fundamentals and 18 Ways to Speed Up Blender Cycles Rendering are typical, each serving as a ready answer to a recurring problem. Hacker News contributes a different strand. The Beauty of Bézier Curves is cited as one of the best math and graphics explainers on YouTube, and Ed Catmull, Pixar: Keep Your Crises Small is a 2009 talk people return to for its lessons on managing creative teams.
animation-vfx.p2: For a first watch, UV Unwrapping - Blender 2.80 Fundamentals is the short, official introduction and covers a problem nearly every beginner hits. If you would rather start with ideas than software, The Beauty of Bézier Curves from 2021 works without opening Blender at all. The longer commitment is Blender 3.0 Beginner Tutorial - Part 1, the start of a full course. The rest covers camera tracking, normal baking, microdisplacement, low poly modeling, and some film history, including the 2014 Star Wars featurette on how the lightsaber was made.

chemistry.p1: This is less a chemistry course than a set of links people reach for when a specific subject comes up in a thread. Mention dishwashers and someone posts I messed up. You're using too much detergent. Bring up leaded fuel or corporate negligence and The Man Who Accidentally Killed The Most People In History appears, with The Biggest Chemical Coverup In History doing the same job for PFAS. Richard Feynman Fire gets cited as a compact explanation of fire and photosynthesis, while Clasp: Common Lisp using LLVM and C++ for Molecular Metaprogramming is the odd one out, a 2015 Google talk programmers share as an example of Lisp used at the edge of science.
chemistry.p2: Start with Richard Feynman Fire, a 2009 clip that is the quickest way to see why people keep passing this list around. The longer commitment is The Chemical History of a Candle by Michael Faraday, which engineerguy splits into six parts beginning with the Introduction. Beyond those, the list runs through practical answers on submarine oxygen and fluorine combustion, NileRed making ferrofluid from scratch, a cluster of 2022 and 2023 videos on infrared cooling paint, and Adam Ragusea on why Hershey bars taste the way they do.

materials-science.p1: This list collects the materials videos that commenters reach for when a thread turns to how a substance actually behaves or gets made. The most persistent is Finding the Missing Memristor - R. Stanley Williams, a 2010 talk people have cited for years as the clearest technical introduction to memristors, given by the researcher whose group found the physical device. Why It Was Almost Impossible to Make the Blue LED gets shared as a story of stubborn persistence behind modern lighting. A cluster of radiative cooling paint builds from Tech Ingredients and NightHawkInLight resurfaces every time those coatings make the news, and Making ferrofluid from scratch serves Chemistry Stack Exchange as a worked synthesis example.
materials-science.p2: For a quick first watch, Mystery of Prince Rupert's Drop at 130,000 fps - Smarter Every Day 86 from 2013 is short and memorable for its high-speed footage, and The Infinite Pattern That Never Repeats is an approachable look at aperiodic tiling that works even with kids. The memristor talk is the longer, denser commitment. Beyond those, the rest runs from iron smelting in Africa and tin pest to liquid metal batteries, jet engine engineering, and a superconductor levitating on a Möbius strip.

cosmology-astrophysics.p1: Most of these 167 videos are answers to recurring questions rather than entertainment. A new way to visualize General Relativity, from ScienceClic in 2020, is what Physics Stack Exchange answerers link when someone has been misled by the rubber-sheet picture of curved spacetime. How to Understand What Black Holes Look Like gets linked for questions about the photon sphere and lensed accretion discs. The Solar Gravitational Lens will Map Exoplanets. Seriously. resurfaces on Hacker News whenever exoplanet imaging comes up. Mixed in are talks people still cite, like Lawrence Krauss's 2009 A Universe From Nothing, and worldbuilding references on sky colour and faster-than-light travel.
cosmology-astrophysics.p2: For a quick first watch, Why is the Solar System Flat? from minutephysics (2014) answers one clean question briefly. Follow it with the ScienceClic relativity video, the most recommended item here. The longer commitment is the Krauss lecture, which Hacker News remembers for the point that distant galaxies will eventually become unobservable, or melodysheep's 2019 timelapse of the far future. The rest ranges from Veritasium on gravity and expansion to Isaac Arthur's Starlifting, the 1977 Powers of Ten, and Sagan's Pale Blue Dot.

fundamental-physics.p1: Most of these 363 videos get linked as answers to questions that keep coming back, usually on Physics Stack Exchange, about why something works the way it does. How Special Relativity Makes Magnets Work is the most cited, used to show a magnetic field as an electric field seen from a moving frame. The Biggest Misconception About Electricity and How Electricity Actually Works settle recurring arguments about where circuit energy flows and the 1/c bulb puzzle. A new way to visualize General Relativity is offered as the fix for misleading rubber-sheet pictures of curved spacetime. Richard Feynman. Why. turns up whenever a question asks for a mechanism beneath a fundamental law.
fundamental-physics.p2: Start with MAGNETS: How Do They Work? from minutephysics or the Veritasium magnet video from 2013, both quick primers on familiar puzzles. The real commitment is the 2015 Gravity and Light winter school with Frederic Schuller, whose lectures, including Newtonian spacetime is curved, build general relativity from logic and geometry upward. Between those sit electricity debates, including AlphaPhoenix testing them with 1000 meters of wire, black hole imaging and lensing, the speed of light, interference energy from MIT, and PBS Space Time on causality.

computer-vision-speech.p1: This is a mixed shelf: deep learning overviews, practical setup guides, signal processing explainers and a few oddities that keep resurfacing in threads. Many are answers to recurring questions. Voice Driven Development: Who needs a keyboard anyway? by Emily Shea gets posted whenever someone asks about coding by voice or working around RSI, and Stack Overflow askers keep landing on OpenCV (All Versions) - Easy Installation Guide and Sample Project (VS 2010 C++) when their builds fail to link. Others are talks people cite as reference points, like Andrej Karpathy - AI for Full-Self Driving at Tesla, which Hacker News uses both to defend and to criticize Tesla's progress.
computer-vision-speech.p2: For a quick first watch, JPEG DCT, Discrete Cosine Transform (JPEG Pt2)- Computerphile is a short, clear introduction that several commenters say finally made the transform make sense. The longer commitment is Tensorflow and deep learning - without a PhD by Martin Görner, about two hours of practical material from 2016. From there the list covers older vision work such as the 2011 Bay Area Vision Meeting talk, spaCy's NER internals, Karpathy's 2024 tokenizer build, homography lectures, and a piano made to speak.

data-science-statistics.p1: This list is mostly practical answers to questions that keep coming back. When someone on Hacker News asks about colormaps or color perception, the reply is usually A Better Default Colormap for Matplotlib | SciPy 2015, a short, funny talk that has been linked more than anything else here. When a shaky study or the p<0.05 threshold comes up, people post Is Most Published Research Wrong? Hans Rosling's DON'T PANIC gets cited against overpopulation alarm, and Stack Overflow users send R programmers fitting a model per group to Hadley Wickham: Managing many models with R. Running through it all is a long argument about notebooks versus testable code.
data-science-statistics.p2: Start with the matplotlib colormap talk from 2015, which commenters describe as brief and clear, or the VisiData Lightning Demo from PyCascades 2018, which shows the tool faster than any written description could. For the heavier stretch, watch I don't like notebooks by Joel Grus and then Jeremy Howard's reply, I Like Notebooks, from 2020. Beyond those, the list covers p values and replication, Michael Stonebraker on big data, reproducible research with org-mode, Pluto.jl, and some unglamorous but useful Excel and Weka material.

physics-space-other.p1: This is a mixed shelf of science explainers that commenters reach for when a particular question comes up again. A large share is about metrology: How We're Redefining the kg and The world depends on a collection of strange items. They're not cheap get posted whenever the kilogram redefinition or NIST's expensive peanut butter reference material appears in a thread. The Physics and Philosophy of Time - with Carlo Rovelli is the lecture people cite in arguments about entropy and the arrow of time. I promise this story about microwaves is interesting, from Tom Scott in 2021, is recommended as a well-told chase of an odd fact that ends with an interview with Lovelock at 101.
