physics-space-other.p2: For a quick first watch, start with Veritasium's 2013 video on the roundest object, which commenters describe as a short, clear explainer of the Avogadro and Planck approaches to the kilogram. The long commitment is Adam Savage's 45-minute 2022 talk on the science of measurement. Beyond those, the list moves toward worldbuilding and planets with Seasonbuilding 101: Axial Tilt, Isaac Arthur on double planets, and a 2013 conference talk on terrestrial planet formation, then closes with smaller pieces from CGP Grey and Tom Scott on paper sizes, daylight saving and tea.

ai-safety-impact.p1: This list is mostly what Hacker News reaches for when a thread about AI risk or automation needs a shared reference. The most cited is What Happened to Horses Is Happening to Us, CGP Grey's 2014 automation explainer, linked for a decade and lately quoted by skeptics as an overconfident forecast. Robert Miles supplies the answers to recurring questions: Intelligence and Stupidity: The Orthogonality Thesis explains why an AI could understand human ethics without sharing them, and Why Would AI Want to do Bad Things? Instrumental Convergence covers why capable systems might misbehave by default. Talks like The A.I. Dilemma and Slaughterbots get cited when a news story touches the same nerve.
ai-safety-impact.p2: For a first watch, Intro to AI Safety, Remastered from 2021 is the usual link for newcomers, and the short Miles videos from 2018 and 2019 follow naturally from it, including Is AI Safety a Pascal's Mugging? The longer commitments are the lectures and talks, such as Eliezer Yudkowsky on why alignment is hard and Sebastien Bubeck's Sparks of AGI from 2023 on early GPT-4. The rest covers ad-driven algorithms with Zeynep Tufekci, AI in education via Derek Muller, and regulation through Lina Khan on the FTC.

data-visualization.p1: This list is mostly answers to questions that keep coming back. The most recommended video, A Better Default Colormap for Matplotlib | SciPy 2015 | Nathaniel Smith and Stéfan van der Walt, is the talk Hacker News cites whenever color perception or colormaps come up, and people describe it as funny, brief and clear. Hans Rosling's 200 Countries, 200 Years, 4 Minutes - The Joy of Stats - BBC and his TED talks get posted as data-driven replies to pessimism about global progress and overpopulation. Wealth Inequality in America appears in nearly every inequality thread. A smaller cluster comes from GIS Stack Exchange, where QGIS 3.14 time handling and map animation demo serves as the standard walkthrough of the Temporal Controller.
data-visualization.p2: Start with the Rosling BBC clip, which is four minutes by its own title and shows why his animated charts still circulate more than a decade after 2010. Follow it with the matplotlib colormap talk. The larger time investment is the conference material, such as Christopher Domas's 2012 talk on dynamic binary visualization. Beyond that the list runs through visual math and machine learning explainers, 3Blue1Brown's epidemic simulation, Drew Berry's biology animations, a couple of advocacy pieces, and practical QGIS tutorials on labels and mapping.

self-driving-cars.p1: This list collects the talks and essays Hacker News reaches for whenever a thread turns to Waymo, Tesla FSD or robotaxis. Most are technical sources people cite to settle arguments: Andrej Karpathy - AI for Full-Self Driving at Tesla is the usual reference for how Tesla's camera-based system works, and the Google Self-Driving Car Project talk from SXSW Interactive 2016 is valued as a candid look at what a real car sees and where it struggles. George Hotz interviews supply the contrarian view on cameras versus lidar. The most recommended entry, How Self-Driving Cars will Destroy Cities (and what to do about it), is the standing counterargument to the whole enterprise.
self-driving-cars.p2: For a quick first watch, CGP Grey's Traffic Has a Perfect Solution. Humans Are the Problem. from 2016 explains traffic flow briefly and clearly. The longer commitments are the Lex Fridman podcasts, especially George Hotz: Comma.ai, OpenPilot, and Autonomous Vehicles from 2019 and the 2022 Karpathy episode. Beyond those, the list runs through Tesla's own Autonomy Day and AI Day presentations, a 2018 MIT lecture from Waymo's Sacha Arnoud, Karpathy's CVPR 2021 keynote, and an IEEE Spectrum explainer from 2011 on Google's early car.

llms-generative-ai.p1: This list is mostly answers to one question that comes up in almost every Hacker News thread about language models: how do these things actually work? The most cited replies are Andrej Karpathy's Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out. and his [1hr Talk] Intro to Large Language Models, along with 3Blue1Brown's visual chapters on transformers and attention, which many commenters say finally made embeddings and attention click. A Hackers' Guide to Language Models by Jeremy Howard is offered as the practical counterpart. A few talks, like Sparks of AGI: early experiments with GPT-4, get cited mainly for specific claims.
llms-generative-ai.p2: For a first evening, start with the 3Blue1Brown transformer chapter, then the attention chapter if text explainers have lost you before. Karpathy's one-hour talk is the dense overview people point to for scaling and training. The real commitment is building GPT in code, and Let's build the GPT Tokenizer adds about two more hours. Beyond those, the list includes older material like the 2017 Attention Is All You Need walkthrough, plus AI risk talks and odd generative experiments such as GAN Theft Auto.

ai-data-other.p1: This is a grab bag of 29 videos that do not fit neatly elsewhere in AI and data: talks on AI history and criticism, search and SEO, recommender systems, and a few demos. Some are answers to a recurring question, like Cloaking, which Webmasters Stack Exchange answerers cite as Google's own word on serving different content to Googlebot. Others are references people reach for in arguments. Colonel JD AI Codec Conversation MGS2 HD comes up whenever AI-generated junk is discussed, and Kenneth Stanley's Machine Learning Street Talk interview on why greatness cannot be planned is the most recommended, valued for reframing goals and open-ended search.
ai-data-other.p2: A good first watch is Hound Internal Demo from 2015, which commenters remember for its speed and as an early look at voice search. The long commitment is The Lighthill Debate (1973) - part 1 of 6, a multipart record of an early fight over AI's prospects. Between those sit Google talks like Human Computation, Soren Johnson's 2010 talk on game AI built to be fun rather than to win, Manipulating the YouTube Algorithm - (Part 1/3) Smarter Every Day 213, and older warnings about filter bubbles and algorithms at scale.

computer-architecture.p1: This list mixes hardware tutorials with conference talks that programmers cite when explaining why code behaves the way it does. Two kinds of recommendation dominate. The first is answers to recurring Stack Overflow questions. Floating Point Numbers - Computerphile gets linked whenever someone asks why 0.1 + 0.2 comes out wrong, and C++ and Beyond 2012: Herb Sutter - atomic Weapons 1 of 2 is the standard reference on memory ordering. The second is Hacker News pointing people to build-it-yourself material. 8-bit computer update launched Ben Eater's breadboard CPU series, and The Ultimate Game Boy Talk (33c3) is the usual starting point for emulator writers.
computer-architecture.p2: For a quick first watch, the 2014 Computerphile floating point video explains its one idea plainly and without much jargon. The long commitment is Ben Eater's work: the 8-bit computer series from 2016 and his 6502 Hello World series from 2019 both reward finishing. Beyond those, the list covers the Apollo Guidance Computer in two well-loved talks, cache behaviour through Scott Meyers, memristors from the researcher who found the device, and security talks on x86 instructions and the Xbox One.

audio-video-engineering.p1: This is mostly a list of explainers that get posted as answers to the same few arguments. The most cited is D/A and A/D | Digital Show and Tell (Monty Montgomery @ xiph.org), which Hacker News treats as the standard rebuttal to audiophile myths and the stair-step picture of digital audio. Floyd Toole - Sound reproduction - art and science/opinions and facts is the talk people cite on speaker accuracy and blind listening tests. Why is TV 29.97 frames per second? turns up whenever that odd number does. Alongside these sit format histories from Techmoan, Ben Eater's hardware build, and a Music Stack Exchange favorite on Strat tremolo setup.
audio-video-engineering.p2: For a short first watch, try Why is TV 29.97 frames per second? from 2016, which commenters praise for its clarity. The Toole lecture from 2015 and the Digital Show and Tell are the heavier sittings, and the latter rewards attention as a primer on sampling. The World's Worst Video Card? explains video hardware with only basic logic assumed. The rest covers MiniDisc and cassettes, the Tefifon, Atari's Quadrascan vector displays, e-paper refresh hacking, segmented displays, and a binaural headphone demo from 2007.

embedded-diy-electronics.p1: This list is less about gadget builds than about the explanations people reach for when a question keeps coming back. The most cited is Sensor Fusion on Android Devices: A Revolution in Motion Processing, a 2010 Google TechTalk that Stack Overflow users link whenever someone tries to integrate accelerometer data twice to get position. Electronics Stack Exchange answerers lean on EEVblog #859 - Bypass / Decoupling Capacitor Tutorial to explain capacitor values and placement. On Hacker News, Ben Eater's 8-bit computer update and The world's worst video card? come up as the clearest way to learn how CPUs and video hardware actually work, explained from basic logic upward.
embedded-diy-electronics.p2: For a quick first watch, pick one of the EEVblog answers, such as the 2015 episode on powering a micro with no power pin, which shows how ESD protection diodes can feed an unpowered chip through its signal pins. The long commitment is Ben Eater, whether the breadboard 8-bit computer series that began in 2016 or the 2019 6502 build. Beyond those, the 206 videos cover Tom7's NES hack, the WIRED Shenzhen documentary, reverse polarity protection, optocouplers on the Raspberry Pi, and extruder calibration.

pure-mathematics.p1: This list is dominated by 3Blue1Brown, whose animated explanations get linked whenever someone on Hacker News or Mathematics Stack Exchange asks what a piece of mathematics actually means. But what is the Fourier Transform? A visual introduction is the most cited, often credited as the explanation that finally made it click. Euler's formula with introductory group theory and Why is pi here? And why is it squared? A geometric answer to the Basel problem turn up as answers to recurring questions about complex exponents and zeta(2). The Essence of linear algebra chapters, especially The determinant, work as a companion to a textbook. These are intuition-builders, not courses with exercises.
pure-mathematics.p2: For a first evening, the Fourier transform video from 2018 is the natural start, followed by The essence of calculus if you want the derivative and integral relationship laid out geometrically. The real commitment is the Essence of linear algebra series from 2016, which runs from a preview and Vectors past Chapter 14 on eigenvectors. Beyond that, the list covers analytic continuation of the zeta function, topology, a 2020 introduction to geometric algebra, and older finds like Moebius Transformations Revealed from 2007.

probability-game-theory.p1: This list is mostly made of answers to questions that keep coming back in comment threads. When a discussion turns to why the US has two parties, someone links Why Your Vote Doesn't Count, CGP Grey's 2011 explainer of first-past-the-post, often alongside The Voting System That Should Replace Every Election. When a Stack Overflow question seeds with srand(time(NULL)) or reaches for rand() with a modulus, rand() Considered Harmful is the standard reply. Bayes theorem, the geometry of changing beliefs is what Cross Validated points people to for conditional probability and the base-rate fallacy. Veritasium's game theory and luck videos fill out threads on cooperation, meritocracy and startups.
probability-game-theory.p2: For a quick first watch, start with Why Your Vote Doesn't Count, which is short and gets cited more than anything else here. The rand() talk from 2013 asks more of you and is aimed at C++ programmers. From there the list splits roughly in three: voting systems, Bayesian reasoning through 3Blue1Brown and The Bayesian Trap, and game theory, where the Golden Balls split or steal clip serves as a real-world prisoner's dilemma. Stand-up Maths on the Dream speedrun case shows probability used to detect cheating.

information-theory.p1: This list is mostly Fourier analysis, with a few practical detours into how computers store numbers and text. The top pick by a wide margin is 3Blue1Brown's But what is the Fourier Transform?  A visual introduction., which Hacker News commenters treat as the default answer whenever someone asks how the transform really works. Floating Point Numbers - Computerphile and Characters, Symbols and the Unicode Miracle - Computerphile show up differently, as links in Stack Overflow answers to recurring questions about 0.1 + 0.2 and garbled UTF-8. D/A and A/D | Digital Show and Tell is the talk people cite to settle arguments about audiophile myths and the stair-step picture of sampled audio.
information-theory.p2: Start with the 3Blue1Brown Fourier Transform video from 2018, then follow it with the same channel's piece on the more general uncertainty principle, which Physics Stack Exchange users use to show the principle comes from wave math. The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT): Most Ingenious Algorithm Ever? from Reducible covers the algorithm itself. The bigger commitment is engineerguy's four-part series on a 100-year-old mechanical computer. Further down are JPEG's discrete cosine transform, Fourier optics, and a 2007 talk on Dasher text entry.

hardware-other.p1: Most of this list is practical bench knowledge, and most of it comes from EEVblog. Electronics Stack Exchange answerers link EEVblog #279 - How NOT To Blow Up Your Oscilloscope! whenever someone has a question about scope grounding or has just destroyed something with a ground clip. EEVblog #453 - Mysteries of x1 Oscilloscope Probes Revealed and EEVblog #317 - PCB Tinning Myth Busting get cited the same way, as settled answers to questions that keep coming up. Hacker News contributes the storage oddities: Harder Drive: Hard drives we didn't want or need, which people share as silly but genuinely educational computer science.
hardware-other.p2: Start with Shouting in the Datacenter, the 2008 clip that Hacker News brings up whenever vibration or sound affecting hard drives comes up. Harder Drive from 2022 is a longer, looser watch. The real commitment is the Rick Hartley session on PCB layer ordering and stackup, which suits people actually laying out boards. The rest is reference material: power supply ripple, MOSFET models built from datasheet curves, why digital scopes look noisy, and a 2022 animated explanation of computer memory.

algorithms-data-structures.p1: Most of these 169 videos are conference talks that programmers cite when an argument turns to how data structures behave on real hardware. Chandler Carruth's CppCon 2014 talk on efficiency and performance is the most cited, usually to explain why std::vector beats linked structures and std::map. Hash tables get the most attention overall. Modern Dictionaries by Raymond Hettinger and PyCon 2010: The Mighty Dictionary are linked on Stack Overflow whenever someone asks why Python dict order looks the way it does, and Matt Kulukundis's 2017 talk is the standard reference for SwissTable. Lecture 19: Dynamic Programming I: Fibonacci, Shortest Paths fills the classroom role.
algorithms-data-structures.p2: For a first evening, The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT): Most Ingenious Algorithm Ever? from Reducible (2020) is a self-contained explanation that commenters say made the idea click. The freeCodeCamp dynamic programming course from the same year is the long commitment, a full course of worked problems like grid traveler and canConstruct. Beyond those, the list covers immutable and persistent data structures, sorting performance, A* pathfinding, and lighter material such as quick-sort performed as a Hungarian folk dance and suckerpinch's chess algorithms.

quantum-computing.p1: This is a small list of 18 videos, and it is dominated by one answer to a question that keeps coming up on Hacker News: where should a programmer start with quantum computing? The usual reply is Quantum Computing for Computer Scientists from Microsoft Research, recommended in 16 comments because it skips the pop-science analogies and asks only for basic linear algebra. Around it sit explainers people cite when Shor's algorithm and encryption come up, such as How Quantum Computers Break Encryption | Shor's Algorithm Explained from minutephysics and two PBS Infinite Series episodes, plus 35C3 - The year in post-quantum crypto for the cryptography side.
quantum-computing.p2: For a quick first watch, the minutephysics Shor video from 2019 or WIRED's Quantum Computing Expert Explains One Concept in 5 Levels of Difficulty will tell you whether the subject holds your interest. The Microsoft Research lecture is the real commitment, best watched with pen and paper. After that the list spreads out: Qiskit coding episodes on Grover's algorithm and the variational quantum eigensolver, a Peter Shor interview, a lecture on the CHSH inequality, Urmila Mahadev on classical verification, and a 2011 Scott Aaronson TEDx talk.

labor-work-wealth.p1: This is less a syllabus than a set of standing answers to arguments that recur on Hacker News: will automation take our jobs, how unequal is wealth really, why is the middle class squeezed, and can America still make things. What Happened to Horses Is Happening to Us has been the default reply on automation for a decade, though skeptics now point to it as an overconfident prediction. Wealth Inequality in America gets dropped as a quick visual of perceived versus actual distribution. Talks people cite fill out the rest, including Winners Take All, a critique of philanthropy delivered inside Google, and Elizabeth Warren's 2008 lecture on the collapse of the middle class.
labor-work-wealth.p2: Start with the CGP Grey video from 2014 or the politizane chart animation from 2012, both short and easy to argue with afterward. The longer commitment is the Warren lecture, which commenters value for its data, or Richard Wolff's 2017 case for worker cooperatives. From there the list spreads out: Milton Friedman on the negative income tax, the gumball demonstration on immigration and global poverty, the People Make Games investigations into Roblox and young developers, San Francisco housing fights, and Smarter Every Day's 2025 attempt to manufacture a product in America.

tech-industry-business.p1: This is a shelf of explainers and critiques that commenters reach for when a thread turns to who controls the platforms and why. Most are answers to a recurring question. Tom Scott's YouTube's copyright system isn't broken. The world's is. gets linked in nearly every takedown argument, VidMe or Why Platforms Aren't Your Friends comes up whenever someone asks why a YouTube or Reddit alternative failed, and All-In Summit: Bill Gurley presents 2,851 Miles is the standard citation for regulatory capture. Others are talks people cite as arguments, such as Anand Giridharadas delivering his critique of win-win philanthropy at Google in 2018.
tech-industry-business.p2: Start with the Tom Scott video from 2020, the most recommended item here and a compact, complete explanation of automated copyright enforcement. The long commitment is Line Goes Up - The Problem With NFTs from 2022, the long-form crypto critique skeptics point to when they want something thorough. Between those, two John Oliver segments cover net neutrality and Sinclair's scripted local news, and the remainder covers Facebook's fake likes and view counts, Roblox's treatment of young developers, Peter Thiel's case against competition, and tech surveillance.

startups-entrepreneurship.p1: This list is mostly talks that Hacker News commenters use to answer the same few questions about building a company. Designing the Ideal Bootstrapped Business with Jason Cohen is the standard reply when someone asks about SaaS pricing or whether to bootstrap instead of raising VC. Mike Monteiro: F*ck You, Pay Me gets sent to freelancers whenever a client stops paying. David Heinemeier Hansson at Startup School 08 has been the touchstone for skeptics of hyper-scale startup culture for over a decade. Darius Kazemi, Tiny Subversions - XOXO Festival (2014) is cited against survivorship-bias success stories. Alongside these sit Y Combinator lectures and a few cautionary hardware stories.
startups-entrepreneurship.p2: A reasonable first watch is Jeff Bezos - Regret Minimization Framework, a single decision rule people pass around, or Monteiro's 2012 talk if you do client work. The longer commitments are the documentaries: Shenzhen: The Silicon Valley of Hardware (Full Documentary) from 2016 and the Makani feature film from 2020. Between those you get Peter Thiel's 2014 Competition is for Losers lecture, Paul Graham's 2012 keynote, the AvE Juicero teardown, and Austin Meyer's account of patent trolling.

logic-formal-methods.p1: This is a mix of conference talks and popular math videos that programmers and mathematicians keep handing to each other when the same questions come up. Brian Beckman: Don't fear the Monad is the standard reply when someone asks for a monad explanation that actually works, and several commenters say it was the one that made the idea click. Propositions as Types by Philip Wadler shows up in favorite-talk threads as the case for why logic and functional programming are the same subject. The Future of Mathematics? from Microsoft Research is cited when proof assistants and formalizing mathematics come up, and 28c3: The Science of Insecurity is the usual introduction to LANGSEC in security discussions.
logic-formal-methods.p2: For a quick first watch, Math's Fundamental Flaw from Veritasium (2021) gives an accessible account of incompleteness, and Vsauce's How To Count Past Infinity covers cardinals and ordinals for a lay audience. The long commitment is Frederic Schuller's 2015 lecture on the logic of propositions and predicates, which opens a rigorous series that continues into differential geometry. The rest runs from Leslie Lamport on thinking above the code and a Strange Loop talk on finding bugs without running code to Edwin Brady's talks on Idris 2 and type-driven development.

macroeconomics.p1: This is less a syllabus than a set of standing answers to questions that come up again and again in threads about debt, inflation, cities and global finance. The most recommended is How The Economic Machine Works by Ray Dalio, offered whenever someone asks for a layperson's explanation of credit and economic cycles. Fear the Boom and Bust: Keynes vs. Hayek gets passed around as a funny but accurate primer on two views of the business cycle. Why American Cities Are Broke - The Growth Ponzi Scheme is the go-to explanation of how low-density infrastructure is financed, and Hans Rosling's 200 Countries, 200 Years, 4 Minutes is sent as a short corrective to cynicism about global progress.
macroeconomics.p2: Start with the Rosling BBC clip, which is four minutes, or the 2010 Keynes vs. Hayek rap battle and its 2011 sequel. Dalio's 2013 video is the natural next step for the mechanics of debt, and his 2022 Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order is the larger commitment, placing the present inside long debt and empire cycles. Beyond that, the list covers the Not Just Bikes Strong Towns series on municipal finance, offshore finance in The Spider's Web, money creation, energy and growth, and a Margin Call scene.

microeconomics-behavioral.p1: This is less a course in economics than a set of links people reach for when a thread turns to money, incentives or policy. Some settle recurring arguments: Longer-lasting light bulbs: it was complicated is the standard reply whenever someone raises the lightbulb conspiracy, and Tobacco: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO) shows up in trade-deal threads as a plain example of ISDS. Others are talks people cite and return to, like Charlie Munger's The Psychology of Human Misjudgement, which commenters rewatch every few years, or David Graeber's Debt: The First 5,000 Years, offered as a different account of what money is.
microeconomics-behavioral.p2: The quick first watch is Fear the Boom and Bust: Keynes vs. Hayek, the 2010 rap video that HN treats as a funny and fairly accurate primer on two views of the business cycle. Graeber's talk is the longer commitment at about 80 minutes, and the Thiel episode of The Portal is similarly wide-ranging. The rest mixes explainers on airline classes, carbon offsets and nuclear reactor costs with arguments about policy, from Milton Friedman on the negative income tax to Richard Wolff on worker cooperatives.

management-leadership.p1: This is less a management curriculum than a set of videos people link when a workplace argument needs settling. Try to Rule Fairly and You'll Be Overthrown gets cited as the short version of how power and incentives work, in governments and companies alike. RSA ANIMATE: Drive: The surprising truth about what motivates us is the standard answer on Software Engineering Stack Exchange whenever pay, bonuses or retention come up. The Only Unbreakable Law is the usual link for Conway's Law, and Richard Cook's Resilience In Complex Adaptive Systems is the talk people reach for to explain normalization of deviance and how systems drift toward failure.
management-leadership.p2: For a quick first watch, start with the CGP Grey video from 2016, then Drive from 2010, the two most recommended items here. The longer commitments are the conference talks: Cook at Velocity NY 2013, Ed Catmull: Keep Your Crises Small at Stanford in 2009, and Bryan Cantrill on Principles of Technology Leadership. The rest runs from Simon Sinek's talks on leadership and millennials to remote work advice, a brief Scrum introduction, The Myth of the Genius Programmer, and engineering culture at NASA and SpaceX.

business-economics-other.p1: This is mostly a list of explainers that Hacker News commenters reach for when the same questions keep coming back: why American rail is slow, why airlines split cabins into classes, why the 747 and A380 faded, and whether drone delivery ever worked. Wendover Productions dominates, with The Economics of Airline Class, Big Plane vs Little Plane (The Economics of Long-Haul Flights) and Why Trains Suck in America each cited across many threads. Alongside them sit case studies people link as shorthand in arguments, such as How Harley-Davidson Killed Itself and I Tried To Make Something In America (The Smarter Scrubber Experiment), the 2025 video now standard in US manufacturing debates.
business-economics-other.p2: For a quick first watch, Why Trains Suck in America from 2016 is short and gets straight to the point that freight takes priority. The bigger commitment is working through the Wendover set on aviation and logistics, from ETOPS to overnight shipping, which rewards watching in sequence. The rest ranges widely: CGP Grey on what post codes actually encode, Mark Rober on Zipline's medical drones, Patrick Boyle's skeptical take on Neom, and a 2013 60 Minutes piece on Luxottica and who really makes your glasses.

gaming-culture.p1: Despite the gaming label, most of what Hacker News recommends here is about people rather than play: how communities form, turn on someone, or get sold something. In Search Of A Flat Earth from Folding Ideas leads the list as the documentary commenters point to for understanding why people fall into conspiracy theories. This Is Phil Fish gets cited in threads about harassment and internet fame, and Contrepreneurs: The Mikkelsen Twins comes up whenever book spam or passive-income hustles are discussed. These are essays people cite as the standard reference on a recurring argument, alongside a smaller set of Minecraft and tabletop how-to answers from Stack Exchange.
gaming-culture.p2: For a short first watch, The Engoodening of No Man's Sky (2020) is the easy entry, an entertaining account of a failed launch and its recovery that commenters bring up around Star Citizen. The longer evening is the Folding Ideas run: the flat earth film, Contrepreneurs, and This is Financial Advice from 2023. Beyond those, the list moves through People Make Games reporting on Roblox and Steam gambling, older criticism like Sequelitis from 2011, Matthew Colville on player types, and practical Minecraft tutorials.

game-history-retro.p1: This is mostly a list about working inside hard limits. Hacker News commenters reach for these videos when a thread turns to old hardware, clever hacks, or how a classic game was made. How Crash Bandicoot Hacked The Original Playstation is the go-to reference for squeezing performance out of a console. The Ultimate Game Boy Talk (33c3) is treated as the standard starting point for emulator writers. SNES Code Injection -- Flappy Bird in SMW gets cited whenever arbitrary code execution comes up. GDC's classic game postmortems, such as 'Diablo': A Classic Game Postmortem, round it out as talks people quote.
game-history-retro.p2: For a first watch, start with the 2013 suckerpinch video Computer program that learns to play classic NES games, which is funny and easy to follow. Then try How we fit an NES game into 40 Kilobytes. The 33c3 Game Boy talk and GET LAMP: The Text Adventure Documentary are the longer evenings. The rest covers N64 code rewrites, pinball machines, Civilization's origins, and the No Man's Sky recovery, plus a few one-off links answering identify-this-show questions.

game-design.p1: This list is mostly conference talks that developers keep citing to each other, plus a few practical answers from Stack Exchange. The most linked is Juice it or lose it - a talk by Martin Jonasson & Petri Purho, the standard reply when someone asks how to make an interactive thing feel good. Preventing the Collapse of Civilization travels well beyond games, turning up in threads about software decay and lost knowledge. Failing to Fail: The Spiderweb Software Way gets passed around for its funny account of running a long-lived indie studio, and Exploring the Tech and Design of Noita is the reference for anyone building falling-sand simulations.
game-design.p2: Start with Juice it or lose it from 2012, then the Vlambeer screenshake talk from 2013. Both show a bland prototype becoming satisfying step by step, and they pair naturally. The bigger commitment is the Jonathan Blow material, which runs from 2011 to 2019 and moves from game design as a medium to civilizational fragility. The rest covers GDC postmortems like Diablo and DOOM's music, Sequelitis on Mega Man, Folding Ideas on Fortnite's monetization, tabletop advice from Matthew Colville, and some Minecraft and Unity tutorials.

speedrunning-glitches.p1: This is less a speedrunning list than a collection of videos about how games actually work under the hood, which is why programmers keep passing them around. SM64 - Watch for Rolling Rocks - 0.5x A Presses (Commentated) [OUTDATED] is the usual citation when someone asks for a lucid, funny explanation of game internals. SNES Code Injection -- Flappy Bird in SMW comes up whenever arbitrary code execution through gameplay needs a canonical example. MarI/O - Machine Learning for Video Games serves as the standard primer on neuroevolution, and Reverse emulating the NES to give it SUPER POWERS! gets linked as a deadpan, inventive hardware hack. Most of these are references people reach for in threads, not background viewing.
speedrunning-glitches.p2: For a short first watch, the SethBling videos are the easy entry: MarI/O from 2015 or the Flappy Bird injection from 2016. The pannenkoek2012 video is the bigger commitment, and it tends to lead into the rest of that channel, including Walls, Floors, & Ceilings. Kaze Emanuar's 2022 work on the SM64 source covers N64 bus contention and optimization. Beyond that the list branches into statistics on the Dream Minecraft controversy, the MyHouse.WAD story, Summoning Salt's Choco Mountain history, and Kerbal save file editing.

investing-personal-finance.p1: This is less a finance curriculum than a set of videos Hacker News reaches for when the same arguments come back around: index funds versus stock picking, renting versus owning, crypto skepticism, and how money is actually created. Jim Simons (full length interview) - Numberphile is the most cited, valued for how much credit Simons gives to luck. The Psychology of Human Misjudgement - Charlie Munger Full Speech is the talk people say they rewatch every few years. This is Financial Advice resurfaces whenever GameStop is in the news, and How Bitcoin Works Under the Hood is a standing answer on Bitcoin Stack Exchange whenever someone needs the basics of transactions and double spending.
investing-personal-finance.p2: For a short first watch, try the Margin Call senior partners scene or Ben Felix's 2019 Renting vs. Buying a Home: The 5% Rule, both narrow and self-contained. The longer commitment is MIT OpenCourseWare's 2013 course, which opens with Ses 1: Introduction and Course Overview. JL Collins's 2018 Google talk covers plain index fund investing. The rest moves between monetary history with a goldbug slant, Coffeezilla on Tether, Bill Gurley on regulatory capture, and John Oliver on predatory lending.

psychology-behavior.p1: This list is mostly what people link when a thread turns to why humans do what they do. The most cited is RSA ANIMATE: Drive: The surprising truth about what motivates us, which Stack Exchange answerers post whenever developer pay, bonuses or retention comes up, as evidence that money stops motivating once basic needs are met. Introduction to Human Behavioral Biology is the lecture series people actually finish and then push on others. The Century of the Self turns up in threads about advertising and propaganda, while Essential Ideas for Parents is offered as the thing to watch before arguing about ADHD.
psychology-behavior.p2: For a quick first watch, try The 7 Habits of Highly Miserable People from CGP Grey or the RSA Drive animation from 2010, both short and easy to finish in a sitting. The long commitment is the Stanford behavioral biology course from 2011, a full lecture series, with Adam Curtis's multi-part documentary close behind. The rest covers motivation and dopamine through Andrew Huberman, status through Alain de Botton, Charlie Munger on misjudgement, Randy Pausch's Last Lecture from 2007, and Russell Barkley on treating ADHD.

neuroscience-brain.p1: Most of what gets recommended here is practical brain science that commenters hand to each other in response to a specific complaint: can't sleep, can't focus, feeling low, curious why people behave as they do. Robert Sapolsky anchors the list. Introduction to Human Behavioral Biology is the lecture series people actually finish and keep pointing others toward, and Stanford's Sapolsky On Depression in U.S. (Full Lecture) is the standard reply when someone asks how depression works. Sleep threads keep surfacing Dr. William Dement's Google talk and Joe Rogan Experience #1109 - Matthew Walker. Further out, What Bodies Think About: Bioelectric Computation Outside the Nervous System - NeurIPS 2018 gets cited as the entry point to Michael Levin's work on bioelectricity.
neuroscience-brain.p2: For a short first watch, try Why You Should Put YOUR MASK On First (My Brain Without Oxygen) from SmarterEveryDay, a 2016 demonstration of hypoxia quietly wrecking judgment that comes up in threads on flying and diving. The long commitment is Sapolsky's 2011 Stanford course, which runs to many lectures. In between are Andrew Huberman's episodes on dopamine, sleep and alcohol, CGP Grey on split brains, Rick Beato on perfect pitch, and Donald Hoffman's TED talk on perception. The TEDx porn talk is popular but its science is disputed.

biology-biotech.p1: This list is mostly what commenters post when a biology thread needs a reference point. Michael Levin's What Bodies Think About: Bioelectric Computation Outside the Nervous System - NeurIPS 2018 is the most cited, offered as the way into his work on bioelectricity and regeneration. Joe Rogan Experience #1035 - Paul Stamets shows up whenever fungi or mycelium come up. DEF CON 25 - John Sotos - Genetic Diseases to Guide Digital Hacks of the Human Genome gets linked in threads on DNA testing and CRISPR, and I Genetically Engineered *MYSELF* to Fix Lactose Intolerance is the usual example of DIY gene editing.
biology-biotech.p2: For a short first watch, try the Drew Berry and Etsuko Uno DNA animation or The Inner Life of the Cell Animation, both of which show how mechanical and crowded molecular biology really is. The long commitment is Jack Szostak's 2012 lecture series on the origin of cellular life, or the Stamets podcast episode. The remainder covers mRNA translation, the square-cube law, sky and plant color for worldbuilders, and several 2020 discussions of whether Covid-19 came from a lab.

games-other.p1: This is a grab bag, and it reads like one. The two most cited entries pull in opposite directions: golden balls. the weirdest split or steal ever! is the clip people reach for whenever a thread turns to game theory and someone needs a real case of a prisoner's dilemma being bent by one player, while How Valve is Profiting from Steam's Back-Door Casinos gets linked as careful reporting on skin gambling and its reach into minors. Around them sit practical answers from Stack Exchange, such as Minecraft - Tutorial: Hopper Timer for redstone delays and Skill Challenges | Running the Game for anyone running multi-check scenes in D&D.
games-other.p2: Start with the Golden Balls clip from 2012, which is short and makes its point quickly. The Valve piece from 2022 pairs naturally with Coffeezilla's two 2024 videos on Counter-Strike 2 and Valve, plus the Jimquisition on predatory monetization, and together they make the longest sitting here. The rest is reference material you would look up when needed: Dungeons & Dragons rulings from Dragon Talk, Matthew Colville on combat, an iron golem farm guide, Extra Credits on deliberate imbalance, and Shadiversity on what weapons a fairy could wield.

nutrition-diet.p1: These 67 videos are what commenters link when a thread turns to sugar, fasting, seed oils, meat or weight, and they mostly arrive as rebuttals or as the talk someone credits with changing their habits. Sugar: THE BITTER TRUTH, a 2009 UCTV lecture on fructose metabolism, is the most linked YouTube video on Hacker News. Dr. Michael Greger | How Not To Die | Talks at Google gets cited in plant-based and cancer threads, while Nina Teicholz - 'Vegetable Oils: The Unknown Story' supplies the case against seed oils. Eating less Meat won't save the Planet. Here's Why appears as a counterpoint on beef emissions, though its methane argument draws pushback.
nutrition-diet.p2: For a first watch, Is olive oil safe at high heat? Does it taste bad? from Adam Ragusea (2020) answers one practical question. The real commitment is the 2009 sugar lecture, a full university talk that people return to for its detail. From there the list splits into camps: fasting talks from Jason Fung and Pradip Jamnadas, low-carb arguments from Gary Taubes and Sarah Hallberg, plant-based and animal-welfare talks, and Andrew Huberman's 2022 episode on alcohol, which several commenters say got them to drink less.

evolution-genetics.p1: This list gathers the videos commenters link when biology comes up sideways in a thread, as often in passing as in a discussion about evolution itself. The Secret Reason Horses Let Us Ride Them is mostly an answer to a recurring Worldbuilding Stack Exchange question about whether some animal could be domesticated or ridden. DEF CON 25 - John Sotos - Genetic Diseases to Guide Digital Hacks of the Human Genome is the talk people cite in threads on DNA testing, CRISPR and bioweapons. I Genetically Engineered *MYSELF* to Fix Lactose Intolerance serves as the standard example of DIY gene engineering, and mRNA Translation (Advanced) gets linked whenever mRNA vaccines or cell biology come up.
evolution-genetics.p2: For a quick first watch, start with the CGP Grey horse video from 2016 or the Drew Berry and Etsuko Uno DNA animation, which shows the jostling machinery of molecular biology. The long commitment is Jack Szostak (Harvard/HHMI) Part 1: The Origin of Cellular Life on Earth, the opening of a 2012 lecture series on origin-of-life theories. The rest covers game theory and cooperation, evolution and perception, bacteria evolving on a mega-plate, persistence hunting from Attenborough, and a Despacito parody about evo-devo.

chess-board-games.p1: This is less a chess channel roundup than a set of videos about how games get played, solved and learned, by people and by programs. Much of it is game-playing AI: AlphaGo - The Movie | Full award-winning documentary, which commenters value as a human story that non-technical viewers can follow, and suckerpinch's Computer program that learns to play classic NES games and 30 Weird Chess Algorithms: Elo World, cited whenever engines, fuzzing or deliberately weakened play come up. Others answer recurring questions. The Expert Myth gets linked in threads on deliberate practice, and I Solved Klotski explains why some puzzles are hard to navigate.
chess-board-games.p2: For a short, light first watch, Tom Scott vs Irving Finkel: The Royal Game of Ur from 2017 is a friendly match with a curator who clearly loves the subject. The AlphaGo documentary from 2020 is the evening-length commitment. If you want to play better rather than watch machines, John Bartholomew's 2015 Climbing the Rating Ladder: Up to 1000 walks through common mistakes at each level. The rest covers Lichess, a Magic: The Gathering computer, Mario AI, famous games, and a Dungeons & Dragons rules talk.

life-sciences-other.p1: This is a small, mixed shelf of five videos that Hacker News commenters reach for when a specific topic comes up in a thread. Ringing in Ears Tinnitus Treatment is the most recommended, shared by tinnitus sufferers as a free trick that briefly quiets the ringing, with the honest caveat that it is not a cure. Tim Minchin: Storm gets linked in homeopathy arguments for its quotable takedown of alternative medicine. Kauai 'O'o surfaces whenever extinction comes up, as a recording of the last of a species calling for a mate. 327 - Choices, costs, and challenges in US healthcare: insurance, drug pricing, & potential reforms is cited as a primer on where healthcare money goes.
life-sciences-other.p2: Start with the tinnitus video if the ringing is your reason for being here, or with Tim Minchin's Storm from 2011 if you want something funny and short on commitment. The Kauai 'O'o recording from 2009 is brief and stays with you. Todd Becker's 2014 talk on myopia is the one some commenters call life-changing, with a few reporting reduced prescriptions after trying his method. The Peter Attia episode from 2024 is the long commitment, a detailed conversation on insurance, drug pricing, and possible reforms.

mental-health-neurodiversity.p1: This list is dominated by Russell Barkley. His ADHD lectures, uploaded under several names including ADHD: Essential Ideas for Parents - Dr. Russell Barkely and 30 Essential Ideas you should know about ADHD, 1A Intro, Chronic Developmental Disability, get posted whenever a thread turns to ADHD, often with the advice to watch before commenting. Some readers credit This is how you treat ADHD based off science with prompting them to seek a diagnosis. Beside Barkley sits Stanford's Sapolsky On Depression in U.S. (Full Lecture), the standard reply when someone asks what clinical depression actually is. These are lectures people cite as primers, not light viewing.
mental-health-neurodiversity.p2: For a short first watch, try Why Is It So Hard to Do Something That Should Be Easy? from How to ADHD, or Guided Wim Hof Method Breathing, which some commenters use daily for stress. The longer commitment is Barkley's 2012 material, though people say even the first 20 minutes help. The rest covers addiction and alcohol, including Gabor Maté on trauma, a contested TEDx talk on porn, Greg Baugues's 2013 talk on developers and depression, and the Down the Rabbit Hole account of Terry Davis and TempleOS.

renewables-storage.p1: This list is mostly practical explainers that Hacker News and DIY Stack Exchange commenters reach for when the same questions come up again. Technology Connections dominates: Why Heat Pumps are Immensely Important Right Now is the default answer to whether heat pumps actually work, A Complete Beginner's Guide to Electric Vehicles gets linked to show a modest home charging circuit is usually enough, and You are being misled about renewable energy technology. is cited for its figures on solar, batteries, land use and cost. Alongside these sit skeptical counterweights, such as Václav Smil's 2019 talk and Planet of the Humans, which is usually recommended with caveats about its bias.
renewables-storage.p2: For a quick first watch, start with Why Heat Pumps are Immensely Important Right Now, then continue through the rest of that heat pump series, including the ground source episode, if it holds you. The longer commitments are the full-length documentaries: Pulling Power from the Sky, the 2020 film about Makani's airborne wind turbines and their failure, and Planet of the Humans. The rest covers grid interconnection for solar, hydrogen engines, EV lifecycle emissions, vertical farming, and a cooling paint experiment.

climate-science.p1: This is a mixed shelf. Part of it is physical explanation and argument: I Misunderstood the Greenhouse Effect. Here's How It Works. gets linked for its clear handling of the saturation puzzle, and Carl Sagan testifying before Congress in 1985 on climate change turns up as historical record. Part is policy realism, with Václav Smil at Driva Climate Investment Meeting 2019 cited as a data-heavy check on decarbonization optimism. A surprising share comes from Worldbuilding Stack Exchange, where Worldbuilding: How To Design Realistic Climates 1 is the standard answer to a recurring question about placing climate zones on invented planets.
climate-science.p2: The Sabine Hossenfelder video from 2023 is the sensible first watch, since it explains the mechanism the rest of the list assumes. The longest commitment is Joe Rogan Experience #606 with Randall Carlson from 2015, a full podcast episode. After that the list splits. Worldbuilders can work through the Artifexian series on climates, atmospheric circulation and ocean currents. Everyone else gets potholer54's arguments going back to 2008, glacier calving footage, a Climate Town history, and an Everyday Astronaut look at rocket pollution.

climate-debate-policy.p1: These 68 videos are mostly what Hacker News commenters reach for when a climate thread turns into an argument. Many are counterpoints: Václav Smil at Driva Climate Investment Meeting 2019 gets linked as a data-grounded check on techno-optimism, and Eating less Meat won't save the Planet. Here's Why is offered against claims about beef, though some dispute its methane reasoning. Others answer recurring practical questions, as with It’s Time To Break Up With Our Gas Stoves in induction threads, or Life in Syntropy, which people repeatedly call the best introduction to agroforestry. The list includes skeptical films alongside rebuttals, and commenters usually attach caveats.
climate-debate-policy.p2: A sensible first watch is Can YOU Fix Climate Change? from Kurzgesagt (2021), cited for its argument that individual action needs political pressure behind it. Its 2022 follow-up, We WILL Fix Climate Change!, pairs naturally with it. The long commitment is Planet of the Humans, a full documentary from 2020 usually recommended with warnings about bias. Beyond those, the list covers carbon offsets, Allan Savory's contested grazing talk from 2013, Jancovici on energy and growth, and Gwynne Dyer's 2010 lecture on the geopolitics of warming.

geology-earth-science.p1: This is a mixed shelf of 38 videos, and much of it exists because people keep asking the same questions. Great Earthquakes of the Pacific Northwest, a 2016 Central Washington University lecture, is the one Hacker News commenters cite when Cascadia comes up, valued as a dry, hype-free account of the evidence for past quakes. Worldbuilding Stack Exchange answerers send people to Fantasy Maps & Plate Tectonics and its companion on ocean currents when someone needs believable mountains and coastlines. Others are single illustrations people reach for in passing, like Taipei 101 Damper movement on 12 May 08 or the Chasing Ice glacier calving footage. The Randall Carlson Rogan episodes appear too, usually with a note that the ideas are controversial.
geology-earth-science.p2: For a quick first watch, start with the 2008 Taipei 101 damper clip or the Chasing Ice calving footage, both recommended for showing scale. The longer commitment is 4.5 Billion Years in 1 Hour from Kurzgesagt, which commenters credit with giving a real sense of deep time, followed by the Cascadia lecture. The rest runs from Yellowstone supervolcano skepticism and orbits and ice ages to asteroid impact simulations, least cost path analysis, India's water crisis, and how countries measure land area.

film-criticism-analysis.p1: This list splits into two kinds of recommendation. On Hacker News, the links are video essays people cite in arguments. Every Frame a Painting's Jackie Chan - How to Do Action Comedy comes up whenever someone complains about fast-cut Hollywood fight scenes. The Marvel Symphonic Universe is offered as the explanation for why modern film scores sound alike. Kirby Ferguson's Everything is a Remix (Original Series) gets invoked in debates over originality, copyright and AI training. The other half comes from Science Fiction & Fantasy Stack Exchange, where answerers link short clips as evidence. Star Wars Origins: The Dam Busters - Side by Side Scene Comparison, for instance, is used to show where the Death Star trench run came from.
film-criticism-analysis.p2: Start with Jackie Chan - How to Do Action Comedy from 2014, the most recommended video here. Then move on to the other Every Frame a Painting essays from 2015 and 2016, Akira Kurosawa - Composing Movement and Vancouver Never Plays Itself. The long commitment is Jenny Nicholson's The Spectacular Failure of the Star Wars Hotel from 2024, which commenters say holds up despite its length as a case study in misaligned incentives. The rest is Star Wars deleted scenes, a Captain Disillusion breakdown of Flight of the Navigator, and Star Trek warp effect comparisons.

software-other.p1: Despite the catch-all label, this list is mostly mobile and web development material. Stack Overflow answerers link these videos whenever the same question comes up again, so few of them are talks Hacker News argues about. The Problem with Time & Timezones - Computerphile has the widest reach, cited 64 times whenever someone tries to do date arithmetic by hand instead of using a library. When to Use Keys - Flutter Widgets 101 Ep. 4 fixes widgets that hold stale state. Asynchronous Firebase API - Firebase Realtime Database and Android explains why data is null outside onDataChange(). Expanded (Flutter Widget of the Week) settles Row and Column overflow. These are answers to recurring problems, not lectures.
software-other.p2: Start with the 2013 Computerphile timezone video. It is the one item here that applies regardless of what you build. If you write Flutter, watch the Keys and Expanded videos from 2018 together as official explanations of two common layout and state problems. The bigger time investment is the conference sessions, such as Google I/O 2011: Evading Pirates and Stopping Vampires and Single activity: Why, when, and how (Android Dev Summit '18). The rest is older Android material, including the 2013 DevBytes animation videos, a 2009 iPhone tab bar tutorial and Firebase walkthroughs.

software-practice-careers.p1: Much of this list is two kinds of recommendation. One is the Stack Overflow answer that keeps getting written: someone asks why their singleton makes tests painful, and the reply links Google's 2008 Clean Code Talks on global state and unit testing, or Design Tech Talk Series Presents: OO Design for Testability, all arguing for dependency injection. Transforming Code into Beautiful, Idiomatic Python plays the same role for questions about what Pythonic means. The other is the talk Hacker News cites as a reference point, such as TDD, Where Did It All Go Wrong and Bret Victor's The Future of Programming, which commenters treat as near mandatory viewing on testing and on how programming tools stagnated.
software-practice-careers.p2: For a first evening, start with Ian Cooper's 2017 TDD talk, which many commenters say changed how they think about mocks and what a unit is, then follow it with the 2008 Google testing talks, which make the same case from the design side. The long commitment is freeCodeCamp's 32-hour blockchain and Web3 course. The rest of the 564 videos runs from Uncle Bob on programming history to async questions in Flutter and Firestore, reading the jQuery source, and Clojure craftsmanship.

scripting-languages.p1: Most of this list is conference talks that commenters reach for when a familiar question comes up again. What the heck is the event loop anyway? gets linked on Stack Overflow whenever someone is puzzled by setTimeout(fn, 0), lagging React state, or a loop that blocks everything. Stop Writing Classes is the standard reply to a Python class with nothing but __init__ and one other method, and The Problem with Time & Timezones - Computerphile is the usual argument for a date library over hand-rolled arithmetic. Hacker News citations lean toward craft talks people keep calling the best they have seen, such as RailsConf 2014 - All the Little Things by Sandi Metz and Jim Weirich's Y combinator talk from Ruby Conf 12.
scripting-languages.p2: Start with the event loop talk from 2014, recommended far more than anything else here, because it explains behavior you will meet in almost any JavaScript code. The bigger commitment is Andrej Karpathy's 2022 micrograd lecture, which builds backpropagation from scratch in code. Beyond those, the list covers object design and testing from Sandi Metz, Douglas Crockford's JavaScript: The Good Parts from 2009, API design from 2007, idiomatic Python, and Armin Ronacher on why Python's internals make it hard to speed up.

software-architecture-design.p1: Most of this list is answers to questions that keep coming back on Stack Overflow, plus a handful of talks Hacker News cites as standard viewing. Stop Writing Classes gets linked whenever a Python class with an __init__ and one other method would be simpler as a plain function. Google's 2008 Clean Code Talks are the stock answers on singletons, global state, dependency injection and replacing switch logic with polymorphism. How To Design A Good API and Why it Matters is the default reference for interface design. On Hacker News, Rich Hickey's Simple Made Easy and RailsConf 2014 - All the Little Things by Sandi Metz are recommended to programmers in any language.
software-architecture-design.p2: Start with Stop Writing Classes from 2012. It makes one focused argument, and the point carries well beyond Python. The larger commitment is the Clean Code Talks taken as a series, followed by Sandi Metz's two Confreaks talks on refactoring and testing. After that the list widens. It includes Robert Martin's Architecture the Lost Years keynote, Mike Acton on data-oriented design at CppCon 2014, and Richard Feldman's Elm talk on making impossible states impossible. Framework-specific entries on AngularJS, Flutter and Unity are mainly worth watching if you use those tools.

web-development.p1: Most of these 1,768 videos earn their place as answers. Someone on Stack Overflow or Hacker News asks why setTimeout(fn, 0) runs late, how to do joins in Firebase, or why the authorization code goes over the back channel, and a commenter links the same talk instead of retyping it. What the heck is the event loop anyway? leads with 287 recommending comments, followed by Jake Archibald's 2018 JSConf talk on the browser event loop. Denormalization is normal with the Firebase Database and OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (in plain English) do the same work for data modeling and auth. A few, like Rich Harris - Rethinking reactivity, are cited for their ideas.
web-development.p2: Start with Philip Roberts's 2014 event loop talk, then Jake Archibald's 2018 follow-up, which adds microtasks and requestAnimationFrame. The larger commitment is JavaScript: The Good Parts, a 2009 Google TechTalk that commenters treat as the proper starting point for the language's quirks around equality, scoping and prototypes. Past that, the list turns practical: Firestore security rules and geohash queries, Flutter widget keys, OAuth flows, and AngularJS best practices from 2012, which still explain scope rules for anyone maintaining older code.

literature-writing.p1: This list splits into two kinds of recommendation. On Hacker News, the draw is a lecture people cite as having changed how they write: LEADERSHIP LAB: The Craft of Writing Effectively, from UChicago Social Sciences in 2014, leads with 19 recommending comments, and its follow-up, Writing Beyond the Academy 1.23.15, gets the same treatment. Ira Glass on Storytelling 3 comes up as encouragement for creators unhappy with their early work. On Stack Exchange, videos work as answers to recurring questions: Worldbuilding: How To Design Realistic Climates 1 for invented maps, and George R. R. Martin on how he comes up with his characters' names for Westerosi naming.
literature-writing.p2: For a first watch, try The Egg - A Short Story, Kurzgesagt's 2019 animation, or Ira Glass on Storytelling 3. The longer commitment is the 2014 UChicago writing lecture, and if it lands, the 2015 sequel is the natural next step. After that the list wanders through Douglas Adams on extinction and the environment, two uploads of Kurt Vonnegut on the shapes of stories, CGP Grey on Tolkien's wizards and Alexander Pope, a BBC radio adaptation of Neuromancer, and Emacs For Writers.

databases-storage.p1: This list is mostly made of answers to recurring questions rather than talks people pass around for fun. Most of the links come from Stack Overflow, where Firebase and DynamoDB questions get the same few videos in reply. Denormalization is normal with the Firebase Database is the standard explanation of why you duplicate data instead of joining it. How do queries work in Cloud Firestore? explains why certain queries get rejected. AWS re:Invent 2018: Amazon DynamoDB Deep Dive: Advanced Design Patterns for DynamoDB (DAT401) is the reference for single-table design. Hacker News contributes fewer picks, such as The Value of Values with Rich Hickey, which people cite as the talk that changed how they think about immutability.
databases-storage.p2: If you use Firestore, start with What is a NoSQL Database? How is Cloud Firestore structured?, the first entry in a 2018 Firebase series that goes on to cover queries, data structure and security rules. The bigger commitment is the DynamoDB pair from re:Invent 2018: the DAT401 design patterns session and the DAT321 internals talk on replication and consistency. After those, the list spreads out into Will Wilson's 2014 Strange Loop talk on deterministic simulation testing, prepared statements, and a TestDisk walkthrough for recovering lost partitions.

sports-athletics.p1: This is a small list of 46 videos about human performance at its edges, and most of them reach Hacker News sideways, linked in threads that are not really about sports. The 919 Tribute Tour: On-board record lap, Nordschleife. gets cited as the benchmark lap record, even to people who do not follow cars. Are athletes really getting faster, better, stronger? turns up whenever a thread argues about records, body types or equipment. Lars Andersen: A new level of archery is shared as a rediscovered lost skill, though commenters note it is disputed. RAT POISON AND BRANDY: THE 1904 ST. LOUIS OLYMPIC MARATHON. is passed around simply as a funny, well-told story.
sports-athletics.p2: Start with the Porsche lap from 2018, which is one on-board run of a single lap and asks little of you. The long commitment is High Altitude Leadership, a 2009 Talks at Google hour on K2, leadership and summit fever. Between those, the list leans toward climbing, with several Alex Honnold films including Magnus Midtbø's 2022 session. It also has Rodney Mullen's TED talk tying skateboarding to open source, Mark Rober stealing baseball signs with machine learning, a wingsuit entry into a plane in flight, and John Oliver on the NCAA.

linux-open-source-os.p1: This list splits into two kinds of recommendation. On Hacker News, the links are conference talks people cite to settle recurring arguments. The Tragedy of systemd is handed to anyone caught up in the systemd debate, The Real Story Behind Wayland and X - Daniel Stone (linux.conf.au 2013) appears in nearly every Wayland vs X thread, and LISA11 - Fork Yeah! The Rise and Development of illumos gets quoted whenever Oracle behaves badly. On Stack Overflow and Ask Ubuntu, the videos work as practical answers. Introduction to Git with Scott Chacon of GitHub explains HEAD and branches as pointers, alongside walkthroughs for GNU Parallel, TestDisk partition recovery and dual booting.
linux-open-source-os.p2: Start with The Tragedy of systemd from 2019, the most recommended item here and a balanced view of systemd from a BSD perspective. The 2013 Daniel Stone talk pairs well with it as a funny explanation of why X could not be fixed. The Scott Chacon Git introduction from 2011 is the one to sit through properly, since it is thorough. The rest of the 169 videos are mostly hands-on: dual-boot guides, GParted resizing, Jack and PulseAudio setup, a DebConf 14 Q&A with Linus Torvalds, and Linux Plumbers talks.

magic-performance-oddities.p1: This is a set of 38 videos that commenters reach for when a thread needs a concrete example rather than another explanation. Most are answers to recurring questions. Someone asks how attention works and gets selective attention test. Someone wonders whether ordinary headphones can fake positional sound and gets Virtual Barber Shop (Audio...use headphones, close ur eyes). A Stack Overflow learner stuck on pivots gets Quick-sort with Hungarian (Küküllőmenti legényes) folk dance. Others circulate out of affection, like The man with 1,000 Klein Bottles UNDER his house - Numberphile, where Cliff Stoll's earnest, playful manner is the draw. Dani DaOrtiz's 2022 Fool Us act is praised as craft that holds up after you know the method.
magic-performance-oddities.p2: Start with selective attention test, a quick 2010 clip that works best if you watch it cold, then the Klein bottle video as a relaxed second. The longest commitment is likely Derren Brown - The System (Full), which runs as a complete piece rather than a clip. The juggling patterns talk from the National Museum of Mathematics suits anyone who likes math applied to a physical skill. The rest covers Penn & Teller fooling acts, unpickable locks, OK Go's 2010 Rube Goldberg video, Lars Andersen's contested archery and a piano made to speak.

networking-internet.p1: This is less a networking course than a set of links people reach for when the same questions keep coming back. Characters, Symbols and the Unicode Miracle - Computerphile is the answer Stack Overflow gives when text turns into question marks or garbled symbols. DEFCON 17: More Tricks For Defeating SSL is cited on Security Stack Exchange as the primary source for sslstrip and null-prefix certificate attacks. On Hacker News, This Video Is Sponsored By ███ VPN is the standard reply to VPN ad scare tactics, and Net Neutrality: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO) remains the accessible explainer people point to. Most entries are answers, with a few conference talks mixed in.
networking-internet.p2: Start with Learn CORS In 6 Minutes from 2021, or the 2013 Unicode video, which explains a problem most programmers have already hit. The bigger commitment is the conference material: A Day in the Life of a Billion Packets from AWS re:Invent 2013, on why VPC networking does not behave like physical Ethernet, and Michael Caisse's 2016 CppCon talk on Boost.Asio. Beyond those, expect Python socket programming, home router setup, rollback netcode in fighting games, mobile latency, and suckerpinch's Harder Drive as the odd one out.

automotive-ev.p1: This list mixes engineering explainers with a strong streak of argument about how cars shape daily life. The most recommended item is Around The Corner - How Differential Steering Works (1937), a Depression-era instructional film that commenters keep calling the best explanation of a differential ever made. Alongside it sit pieces people link to settle recurring debates: Cities Aren't Loud: Cars Are Loud in threads on noise and EVs, These Stupid Trucks are Literally Killing Us whenever vehicle size comes up, and A New Car UI: How touch screen controls in cars should work in arguments about touchscreens. Most of these are evidence offered mid-discussion rather than casual viewing.
automotive-ev.p2: Start with the 1937 differential film, then pair it with How Differential Gear works (BEST Tutorial) from 2009 to see the same idea explained twice. If you are weighing an EV, A Complete Beginner's Guide to Electric Vehicles from Technology Connections is the larger commitment, and DIY answerers cite it on home charging circuits. The rest runs from transmissions and hydrogen engines to IIHS crash tests, e-bike safety, headlight repair, and Porsche's record Nordschleife lap.

education-learning.p1: This is less a syllabus than a record of what people point each other to when learning goes wrong. Some entries are talks cited in arguments about teaching itself. How to Speak, the 2019 MIT lecture, is treated on Hacker News as the standard advice on giving talks, and Confessions of a Converted Lecturer: Eric Mazur is offered as the case against the lecture. Others are answers to recurring questions on Stack Exchange. Kate Gregory's CppCon 2015 talk on why to stop teaching C gets linked under C-style beginner code, and Loop like a native: while, for, iterators, generators shows up when someone loops over Python lists by index.
education-learning.p2: For a quick first watch, try RSA ANIMATE: Changing Education Paradigms from 2010 or Marty Lobdell - Study Less Study Smart, a 2011 talk on studying. How to Speak is the one to set an evening aside for. The longer commitments are series and courses: 3Blue1Brown's Essence of linear algebra, freeCodeCamp's 2018 Learn Python - Full Course for Beginners, and the WiseOwlTutorials Excel VBA Introduction. The rest leans practical, from Blender texture coordinates to Python classes, with Alan Kay's Doing with Images Makes Symbols covering the constructionist side.

mechanical-engineering.p1: This list leans toward explanations of machines people use every day without understanding. The most recommended is Around The Corner - How Differential Steering Works (1937), which commenters keep calling the best explanation of differentials and a model of teaching. It pairs naturally with the Navy's Basic Mechanisms In Fire Control Computers, cited whenever analog mechanical computation comes up. Technology Connections covers the household side with Detergent packs are kinda wishy-washy (Dishwashers Explained) and The Antique Toaster that's Better than Yours. These are less answers to a single question than favorites that people rewatch and pass along whenever a thread turns to clever design.
mechanical-engineering.p2: Start with the 1937 differential film, which explains one mechanism completely, or The Ingenious Design of the Aluminum Beverage Can for a similar single-object explainer. The dishwasher video is the longer commitment at over 30 minutes, though commenters say it changes minds about how to use one. The fire control computer film comes in several parts and suits an unhurried evening. The rest is practical: Park Tool derailleur and brake guides, a British Airways 747 D-check used as a maintenance reference, and Origins of Precision from Machine Thinking.

3d-printing-cnc.p1: Despite the fabrication label, this list leans heavily on Blender, and most of its recommendations come from Blender Stack Exchange rather than Hacker News. Answerers keep linking the same tutorials to recurring questions: 8 techniques of cutting holes in Blender when booleans leave messy n-gons, Convert Material Displacement to a Mesh with Blender because Blender has no built-in way to do it, and Blender Mesh Intersect Tool as the canonical demo of that command. The 3D printing side shows up through Thomas Sanladerer's extruder calibration guide. The clear Hacker News favorite is DIY Perks' Building a realistic artificial sun (for dark winter days), cited whenever seasonal affective disorder or bright home lighting comes up.
3d-printing-cnc.p2: For a quick first watch, Grant Abbitt's Texture Painting Quick start is billed at three minutes. The 2020 artificial sun build is worth seeing even if you never open Blender, and the 2014 extruder calibration guide is the practical pick for anyone fighting over- or under-extrusion. The longer commitment is Blender Guru's material: the 2020 beginner chair series including UV unwrapping, the 2017 Intermediate Modelling tutorial, and the 2016 PBR materials walkthrough. Darrin Lile's ten-part character modeling series from 2014 sits at the deep end.

ships-ocean.p1: This is a small shelf of 24 videos that commenters reach for when a maritime thread needs grounding in how things actually work. The most cited is How Do Nuclear Submarines Make Oxygen?- Smarter Every Day 251, the standard answer whenever oxygen candles, CO2 scrubbing or submarine air quality come up. Celestial Navigation (instruction video) gets linked as an unusually clear teaching film and as evidence of how good old military training material can be. The NFB documentary SHIPBREAKERS is offered for its close look at dismantling ships, and The Surprising Efficiency of Canal Locks answers a recurring engineering question.
ships-ocean.p2: For a quick first watch, start with the 2021 Smarter Every Day oxygen episode, then follow it with How I Boarded a US NAVY NUCLEAR SUBMARINE in the Arctic (ICEX 2020), which opens a longer series on life aboard a fast attack sub. The biggest time commitment is five hours of BBC Shipping Forecast, meant as calm background. The rest covers logistics and strategy through Wendover Productions, Why Japan had NO Chance in WW2, the Jones Act, and H I Sutton on China's invasion barges from 2025.

making-woodworking-metalwork.p1: Most of these 48 videos are not shop tutorials but films about how things get made, and Hacker News commenters bring them up whenever a thread turns to craftsmanship, manufacturing or self-reliance. Origins of Precision gets cited in machining and chip-fab discussions for explaining how accuracy is bootstrapped from nothing. Dick Proenneke in Alone in the Wilderness surfaces in threads about cabins, solitude and woodworking. The Art of Making a Nixie Tube is passed around as a portrait of one dedicated maker. The most-cited entry is a programming talk, Tim Ewald - Clojure: Programming with Hand Tools, which people name among the best talks for its argument that heavy tooling can hide simpler solutions.
making-woodworking-metalwork.p2: Start with Origins of Precision from 2017, which runs about half an hour. The long commitment is Dan Gelbart's Building Prototypes, an 18-part course from 2013 that commenters treat as the free standard for building precision mechanical things, alongside Clickspring's Antikythera Mechanism and clockmaking series. Between those sit traditional ironmaking in Smelting Iron in Africa (A DEMONSTRATION), primitive drills, knife sharpening, John Dobson on telescopes, and a Stack Exchange favourite testing end grain glue joints. A few Blender modelling tutorials have strayed in on the word sharpening.

tech-figures-interviews.p1: This is a collection of talks and interviews with people who built the field, and most of it gets recommended because commenters treat it as required context. Growing a Language, by Guy Steele and Alan Kay - Normal Considered Harmful are talks people cite whenever language design or the ahistorical habits of software come up. VCF East: Ken Thompson interviewed by Brian Kernighan is passed around for first-hand Unix stories, while Steve Jobs Stanford Commencement Speech 2005 is what people send to graduates and founders at a crossroads. Others, like Introduction to Node.js with Ryan Dahl, answer a recurring question straight from the creator.
tech-figures-interviews.p2: For a quick first watch, the 2005 Stanford speech is short and needs no background. The longest commitment of the core picks is the one-hour Ousterhout talk at Google on A Philosophy of Software Design, which commenters use to decide whether to read the book. Jim Simons (full length interview) - Numberphile from 2015 offers a humbler view of success that leans on luck. Beyond that, the list moves between Hamming on research, Engelbart's 1968 demo, Kay on Ted Nelson, and a few interviews outside computing.

demoscene-retrocomputing.p1: This list is mostly about doing a lot with very little: demoscene productions, size-coding, and talks on squeezing software onto old hardware. The most cited pieces are demos people point to when someone complains about software bloat, chiefly Elevated by RGBA and TBC, a 4K intro that shows up here in two uploads, and A Mind Is Born (256 bytes). Alongside them sit talks commenters cite as references, such as The Ultimate Game Boy Talk (33c3), the usual starting point for emulator writers, and Jason Turner's CppCon 2016 talk on a Commodore 64 game in C++17, recommended as proof that modern abstractions can compile down to tight code.
demoscene-retrocomputing.p2: For a quick first watch, A Mind Is Born from 2017 delivers a song and visuals from a program smaller than a tweet, and Elevated takes only a few minutes more. The bigger commitment is the Game Boy talk or Turner's CppCon session, both full conference presentations. From there the list branches into Ahoy's 2021 history of tracker music, Inigo Quilez painting a landscape with mathematics, CGA graphics, NES size constraints, Amiga assembly tutorials, and CuriousMarc's restoration of the Apollo Guidance Computer.

internet-culture.p1: This is less a nostalgia tour of the 90s web than a set of explanations commenters reach for when a thread turns to platforms, mobs and moderation. This Is Phil Fish (2014) gets cited as the clearest account of how internet fame and outrage work. YouTube's copyright system isn't broken. The world's is. is the default link in takedown threads, with 13 recommending comments. VidMe or Why Platforms Aren't Your Friends answers the recurring question of why YouTube and Reddit alternatives fail or sour, and This is Financial Advice resurfaces whenever GameStop is in the news. Most entries work as answers to arguments that keep coming back.
internet-culture.p2: Start with Will YouTube Ever Run Out Of Video IDs?, a narrow technical question Stack Overflow users link when explaining random base64 IDs. The Problem With Facebook follows as a 2014 look at fake likes and bot activity. The long commitment is the Why Are You So Angry? series from Innuendo Studios, a multi-part analysis of harassment and gaming culture, alongside ContraPoints essays like Incels and Canceling. The rest runs from CGP Grey and Kurzgesagt on platforms to lighter viral pieces such as What Languages Sound Like To Foreigners.

graphic-design-typography.p1: Despite the label, this list leans as much toward text encoding and color math as toward fonts and logos. The most recommended entries are answers to recurring programming questions. Stack Overflow users link Characters, Symbols and the Unicode Miracle - Computerphile when text turns into question marks, Pragmatic Unicode, or, How do I stop the pain? when Python throws a UnicodeDecodeError, and Computer Color is Broken when blended gradients come out too dark. Hacker News adds a second layer of explainers people cite in passing, such as Brown; color is weird for color perception and Stephen Fry Kinetic Typography - Language whenever a grammar argument starts.
graphic-design-typography.p2: For a quick first watch, start with Computer Color is Broken from 2015, a short visual explanation of gamma-encoded RGB. The longer commitments are the conference talks, Pragmatic Unicode from 2012 and Dylan Beattie's Plain Text from NDC Copenhagen 2022. After those, the list turns to craft and history: Tantacrul on designing a music notation font for MuseScore, FarewellEtaoinShrdlu on the end of hot-metal linotype typesetting, Posy on mouse cursor design, and a 2011 Saul Bass pitch for the Bell System logo.

law-policing-justice.p1: Most of these 190 videos are what Hacker News links when the same arguments come back around: what to do if police want to question you, why copyright enforcement works the way it does, why Congress seems stuck. Don't Talk to the Police is the standard answer to the first, posted in thread after thread about interrogations. YouTube's copyright system isn't broken. The world's is. plays the same role in takedown discussions, with Everything is a Remix (Original Series) close behind whenever originality or AI training comes up. Antonin Scalia - On American Exceptionalism gets cited as a clear case for why the American system is designed to be slow.
law-policing-justice.p2: Start with Don't Talk to the Police, a 2012 recording from Regent University School of Law that needs no background. The long commitment is The Cardboard Box Reform - Nixon's Ghost Bill & A Crucial Flaw in Democracy, an extended, evidence-heavy theory of what changed in Congress in the 1970s that people recommend even when they doubt it. Beyond those, the list covers homelessness through Seattle is Dying, civil forfeiture and tobacco via John Oliver, drug policy, patents, anarcho-capitalist ideas of private law, and Dan Geer's 2014 Black Hat talk on surveillance and liability.

space-exploration.p1: Most of what lands here was linked as an answer to a specific question.
