Space Stack Exchange users reach for SpaceX's own Falcon Heavy Test Flight footage when someone asks about booster separation or the Roadster deployment, and for Scott Manley's Could An Astronaut Throw Something From Orbit To Earth? when the ISS deorbit question comes around again, with its worked figure of about 90 m/s. Hacker News behaves differently, citing talks it treats as required viewing: Light Years Ahead | The 1969 Apollo Guidance Computer for its clear account of restartable, robust software, and The Solar Gravitational Lens will Map Exoplanets. Seriously. whenever exoplanet imaging comes up.
space-exploration.p2: Start with Kurzgesagt's 1,000km Cable to the Stars - The Skyhook from 2019, a quick, accessible introduction to tethers and cheaper orbital launch. The long commitment is 34C3 - The Ultimate Apollo Guidance Computer Talk, a full conference talk from 2017 that pairs naturally with the TNMoC lecture. Beyond those, the list runs from Isaac Arthur's megastructure episodes like Orbital Rings and Starlifting, which worldbuilders lean on, to Scott Manley on heat shields, the 2021 Starbase tour with Elon Musk, and Carl Sagan's Pale Blue Dot.

quantum-physics.p1: This is a list of 106 videos that commenters link when someone asks how quantum mechanics actually works, usually as answers on Physics Stack Exchange or in Hacker News threads about entanglement and measurement. On Hacker News the standout is The Quantum Conspiracy: What Popularizers of QM Don't Want You to Know, a 2011 Google TechTalk that programmers keep citing as the talk that made the subject click. Stack Exchange answerers lean on The more general uncertainty principle, regarding Fourier transforms to show uncertainty comes from wave math rather than measurement disturbance, and on Bell's Theorem: The Quantum Venn Diagram Paradox and Sidney Coleman, Quantum Mechanics in Your Face [1994] to explain why hidden variables fail and why textbook collapse is misleading.
quantum-physics.p2: For a quick first watch, try the minutephysics Bell's theorem video or Veritasium's Quantum Entanglement & Spooky Action at a Distance, which HN calls one of the clearest layman explanations of Bell. The longer commitments are the Coleman lecture, the Google talk, and Sean Carroll's 2020 series The Biggest Ideas in the Universe. The rest covers double slit interference with sunlight, magnets, where nucleon mass really comes from, quantum fields with David Tong, the Higgs with Leonard Susskind, and time with Carlo Rovelli.

robotics.p1: This list splits into two kinds of recommendation. On Hacker News, the videos people keep citing are about what robots and drones mean in practice. What Happened to Horses Is Happening to Us, CGP Grey's 2014 automation explainer, has been linked for a decade, lately also by skeptics as an example of overconfident prediction. Slaughterbots comes up whenever autonomous weapons make the news, and Zipline - How Rwanda Built A Drone Delivery Service is the usual example of drones doing real work. The other half answers recurring Stack Exchange questions, such as the Denavit-Hartenberg Reference Frame Layout video that gets sent to anyone whose DH parameter table looks wrong.
robotics.p2: For a first watch, try 7 Minutes of Terror: The Challenges of Getting to Mars, NASA JPL's 2012 piece on how a Mars landing works, then Mark Rober's 2023 Zipline video. The heavier commitment is the technical material: Peter Corke's ENB339 lecture on planar homography and the ROSCon 2012 talk URDF and You. The rest covers ROS control tutorials, Wendover on why drone delivery stalled, Veritasium's maze-solving competition, and a 2007 giant robot build.

machine-learning.p1: Most of what sits here answers one recurring question on Hacker News: how do I actually understand neural networks? But what is a neural network? | Deep learning chapter 1 from 3Blue1Brown is the standard first stop because it makes the math intuitive. Andrej Karpathy's The spelled-out intro to neural networks and backpropagation: building micrograd is where people send anyone who wants backprop explained with intuition and built in code. Alongside those are lecture series people finish, like RL Course by David Silver - Lecture 1: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning, and lectures cited for the math, such as MIT's 16. Learning: Support Vector Machines, which Cross Validated links when someone asks where the Lagrangian comes from.
machine-learning.p2: Start with the 3Blue1Brown chapter from 2017, then its follow-up Gradient descent, how neural networks learn, and the 2024 chapter Transformers, the tech behind LLMs, which many say finally made attention and embeddings click. The long commitment is Karpathy: micrograd first, then Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out. from 2023, both built up in code. The rest covers reinforcement learning through David Silver's course, neuroevolution in SethBling's MarI/O, the 2008 Stanford machine learning lectures, and AlphaGo - The Movie for an evening without math.

repair-teardown.p1: This is a list of teardowns and repair explainers that Hacker News and Stack Exchange commenters reach for when an argument about how something is built, or why it breaks, needs evidence. Most are answers to recurring questions. Longer-lasting light bulbs: it was complicated is the standard reply to the lightbulb conspiracy claim. The REAL Reason McDonalds Ice Cream Machines Are Always Broken comes up in every McFlurry and right-to-repair thread. A Look Inside Apple's $130 USB-C Cable settles why Thunderbolt cables cost so much. AvE's BOLTR: Juicero, Cold Press Juicer for Rich Weirdos is the stock example of overbuilt hardware. A few, like the MacBook Pro drive cable fix, are practical repair answers.
repair-teardown.p2: Start with the Technology Connections light bulb video from 2023. It is the most recommended item here and changes how you read the rest. The Apple cable CT scans make a quick second watch. For something more involved, the Autoline After Hours teardowns of the BMW i3 (2015) and Tesla Model 3 (2018) go into materials and production methods. The remainder mixes AvE and bigclivedotcom teardowns, Louis Rossmann on right to repair and Apple's repair program, and hands-on fixes for bikes and MacBook keyboards.

consumer-devices.p1: Despite the label, this list is less about new gadgets than about how ordinary devices actually work, and why some of them fail. The most cited entry is a 2010 Google TechTalk, Sensor Fusion on Android Devices: A Revolution in Motion Processing, which Stack Overflow answerers link whenever someone tries to get position by integrating accelerometer data twice. Hacker News leans on talks it treats as authoritative, such as Behind the Scenes of iOS Security and Guarding Against Physical Attacks: The Xbox One Story, and on Technology Connections explainers like Detergent packs are kinda wishy-washy (Dishwashers Explained), which people credit with changing their minds about dishwasher use. Most entries are either answers to recurring questions or reference talks cited in arguments.
consumer-devices.p2: A good first watch is The Antique Toaster that's Better than Yours from 2019, a favorite example of chip-free mechanical design, or the 2017 teardown BOLTR: Juicero, Cold Press Juicer for Rich Weirdos. The longer commitments are the dishwasher video, which runs past 30 minutes, and the full 80-minute iPhone keynote from 2007. The rest mixes hardware security talks, practical fixes like the MacBook Pro drive cable repair, an appreciation of MiniDisc, and a case against single-hose portable air conditioners.

electronics-circuits.p1: This list is mostly two kinds of recommendation. On Electronics Stack Exchange, the same videos get linked as standing answers to recurring questions: EEVblog #859 - Bypass / Decoupling Capacitor Tutorial when someone asks why capacitors sit beside every power pin, and EEVblog #279 - How NOT To Blow Up Your Oscilloscope! after a ground clip has done its damage. Hacker News recommends Ben Eater's 8-bit computer update and the series it started as the clearest way to learn how a CPU works, and AT&T Archives: Similiarities of Wave Behavior (Bonus Edition) keeps coming up as a better introduction to waves and transmission lines than anything made since.
electronics-circuits.p2: Start with EEVblog #279, a practical first watch that may save you a probe or a scope. The long commitment is Ben Eater: the 8-bit breadboard computer from 2016 and the 6502 series from 2019, which people build along with and finish. Rick Hartley's grounding training and his differential pairs keynote, both from 2019, are dense sessions for anyone laying out boards. The rest covers op-amps, x1 scope probes, memristors, and where energy in a circuit actually flows, via Veritasium and AlphaPhoenix.

math-theory-other.p1: This is mostly a shelf of visual explanations that people link when a math question keeps coming back in slightly different words. Linear transformations and matrices | Chapter 3, Essence of linear algebra is the most cited, usually offered on Mathematics Stack Exchange to someone who can compute with matrices but cannot picture what the columns do. Moebius Transformations Revealed plays the same role for the Riemann sphere and circle-preserving maps, and Divergence and curl: The language of Maxwell's equations, fluid flow, and more answers the perennial question about the del notation. The physics side leans on Lecture 9: Newtonian spacetime is curved!, which answers routinely cite by timestamp.
math-theory-other.p2: Moebius Transformations Revealed, from 2007, is the easiest first watch: short and wordless enough to make its point before you finish your tea. The longer commitment is the 2015 Gravity and Light winter school, where Lecture 5 on tangent spaces and Lecture 9 belong to a full course on spacetime geometry. Between those sit more 3Blue1Brown chapters on Taylor series and change of basis, an MIT 18.03 differential equations lecture, Steve Brunton's control bootcamp, Numberphile on stars and bars and the Langlands program, and Wildberger's math history.

semiconductors-manufacturing.p1: This list is mostly what people link when someone on Hacker News asks how chips are actually made. The anchor is Indistinguishable From Magic: Manufacturing Modern Computer Chips, a 2012 talk still cited as the best in-depth introduction to IC fabrication, usually alongside a wish that someone would update it. The Extreme Engineering of ASML’s EUV Light Source appears whenever EUV or ASML comes up, and Jim Keller: Moore’s Law is Not Dead is the standard reply in threads declaring Moore's Law over. Around them sit stories people pass along for their own sake, like Why It Was Almost Impossible to Make the Blue LED and BobbyBroccoli's series on research fraud.
semiconductors-manufacturing.p2: Start with the 2021 Asianometry EUV video, a focused first watch that explains why lithography is so hard. Branch Education's 2025 video on the EUV photolithography system covers the same machine from another angle. Then take on the 2012 talk, or the Lex Fridman conversation with Keller if architecture interests you more than fabrication; that podcast is the long commitment. The rest runs from the 38C3 talk on chips and geopolitics to Sam Zeloof's homemade silicon, a 6502 reverse-engineering talk, and FPGA CPU builds.

recreational-math.p1: This list is mostly 3Blue1Brown, with a few outsiders that earned their place. The videos work as answers to questions that keep coming back. Someone asks how to get an intuition for the Fourier transform and is pointed to But what is the Fourier Transform? A visual introduction. Someone wants linear algebra to finally make sense and gets Vectors | Chapter 1, Essence of linear algebra. Freya Holmér's The Beauty of Bézier Curves is the standard reply for graphics and game programmers. On Physics Stack Exchange, The more general uncertainty principle, regarding Fourier transforms is linked to show the principle comes from wave math rather than measurement disturbance.
recreational-math.p2: The obvious first watch is the 2018 Fourier transform video, the most recommended entry here. The larger commitment is a series. Vectors opens Essence of linear algebra and The essence of calculus starts another, and people tend to work through them chapter by chapter. The Continuity of Splines (2022) follows naturally from the Bézier video. The rest of the 310 covers neural networks, bitcoin, the Basel problem, the Riemann zeta function, Conway's Game Of Life in APL, and a full length Numberphile interview with Jim Simons.

computational-theory.p1: This list is less a course in computation theory than a set of talks that Hacker News commenters cite whenever the subject comes up in a thread. The most recommended is Ruby Conf 12 - Y Not- Adventures in Functional Programming by Jim Weirich, which people point to as the talk that finally makes the Y combinator click, whether or not you write Ruby. Propositions as Types by Philip Wadler is the usual answer to why logic and functional programming are connected. Alongside them sit demonstrations of Turing completeness in odd places, like On The Turing Completeness of PowerPoint (SIGBOVIK) and the MoVfuscator talk, plus 28c3: The Science of Insecurity, the standard introduction to LANGSEC.
computational-theory.p2: For a quick first watch, start with P vs. NP and the Computational Complexity Zoo from 2014, which commenters call the best short introduction for people with no background. Then try Life in life for the visual idea of a machine simulating itself. Math's Fundamental Flaw from Veritasium (2021) covers incompleteness and self-reference accessibly. The bigger commitment is the lambda calculus group: Weirich's 2012 talk, Tom Stuart's Programming with Nothing, and David Beazley's Lambda Calculus from the Ground Up from PyCon 2019, which together build computation from almost nothing.

indie-game-development.p1: This list mixes two kinds of recommendation. One is the conference talk that Hacker News cites whenever game feel, polish or running a small studio comes up: Juice it or lose it - a talk by Martin Jonasson & Petri Purho, the Vlambeer screenshake talk, and Failing to Fail: The Spiderweb Software Way, which commenters value for its account of a long-lived indie business and what Steam gives back for its 30% cut. The other is the practical answer Stack Exchange users link to recurring questions, such as Unite Austin 2017 - Game Architecture with Scriptable Objects for Unity architecture and the Brackeys tutorials for movement code.
indie-game-development.p2: Start with Juice it or lose it from 2012, then the 2013 screenshake talk. Both show a bland prototype becoming satisfying, and together they make a good first evening. The bigger commitment is Jonathan Blow's 2013 talk on programming independent games, which commenters say applies well beyond games. The Engoodening of No Man's Sky is lighter viewing about a failed launch. The rest of the 159 videos lean practical: Unity tutorials, Blender low poly modeling, Android game performance from 2010, and fitting an NES game into 40 kilobytes.

medicine-disease.p1: Most of this list is diet and metabolism rather than infectious disease, because that is where Hacker News arguments about health keep returning. Sugar: THE BITTER TRUTH, a 2009 university lecture on fructose metabolism, is the most-linked YouTube video on the site, and it sits next to Why We Get Fat: And What to Do About It and Dr. Michael Greger | How Not To Die | Talks at Google. These are talks people cite to settle a recurring thread about what to eat. The longevity and epidemic material, such as We Were Taught to Call Death a Blessing, gets posted as a compact answer when aging or pandemics come up.
medicine-disease.p2: Start with Why Some Diseases Only Traveled One Direction, a short 2015 CGP Grey video that commenters use to summarize the core argument of Guns, Germs, and Steel. The longer commitment is the 2009 sugar lecture, which goes deep into biochemistry. From there the list covers fasting talks by Jason Fung and Pradip Jamnadas, Sapolsky on stress, and a 2020 cluster on COVID that ranges from 3Blue1Brown's Simulating an epidemic to lab-leak debate. Some talks rest on anecdote, and commenters say so.

game-programming-engines.p1: This list mixes two kinds of recommendation. Stack Overflow and Game Development Stack Exchange answerers link practical material when the same question comes up again. Unite Austin 2017 - Game Architecture with Scriptable Objects gets linked for structuring Unity data and events. Google I/O 2010 - Writing real-time games for Android redux covers OpenGL ES, textures and garbage collection. Brackeys' FPS controller tutorial helps people whose copied code misbehaves. Hacker News leans toward talks people cite in arguments, such as RustConf 2018 - Closing Keynote - Using Rust For Game Development by Catherine West. Commenters treat it as the clearest explanation of ECS even for non-Rust programmers. Jonathan Blow, John Carmack and Casey Muratori also come up often on how games should be built.
game-programming-engines.p2: For a first evening, How Crash Bandicoot Hacked The Original Playstation | War Stories | Ars Technica is the easy entry, a 2020 account of squeezing old hardware that HN keeps passing around. The long commitment is Jonathan Blow's 2014 talk on a new programming language for games, plus the Jai series that followed, where you watch a language take shape. Between those sit SIGGRAPH rendering talks on Nanite, a GDC session on Noita, Carmack's QuakeCon 2012 keynote, Unity performance tips and Muratori's 2025 critique of object-oriented design.

environment-agriculture.p1: This list is mostly what Hacker News commenters reach for when a thread turns to how food is grown, what farming does to land and animals, and whether growth can continue indefinitely. The most cited are Treating the Farm as an Ecosystem with Gabe Brown Part 1, The 5 Tenets of Soil Health, offered as a favorite introduction to regenerative agriculture; Dominion (2018) - full documentary [Official], pushed as the way to see what factory farming involves; and The Most IMPORTANT Video You'll Ever See (part 1 of 8), the standing answer whenever exponential growth comes up. Others, like Eating less Meat won't save the Planet. Here's Why, arrive as counterpoints and draw their own critiques.
environment-agriculture.p2: For a quick first watch, How to green the world's deserts and reverse climate change | Allan Savory, a 2013 TED talk, lays out the hopeful and contested grazing argument in one sitting. The long commitments are Dominion, a full documentary, and the eight-part exponential growth series from 2007. Beyond those, the list covers agroforestry in Life in Syntropy, a 2026 case for solar and batteries from Technology Connections, walkable grocery shopping in Amsterdam, rocket pollution, the Salton Sea, and a Crash Course episode on the agricultural revolution.

consciousness-mind.p1: This is a list of talks, explainers and lectures that Hacker News readers pass around whenever a thread turns to how minds work. The most cited is What Bodies Think About: Bioelectric Computation Outside the Nervous System - NeurIPS 2018, which commenters keep calling the best introduction to Levin's work on bioelectricity and regeneration. Analogy as the Core of Cognition is the Hofstadter talk regulars reach for in arguments about concepts and metaphor. George Lakoff: Moral Politics gets recommended to people who want to understand why political opponents are not simply stupid. Most entries are citations dropped into an ongoing debate rather than answers to a single question.
consciousness-mind.p2: Start with You Actually Share Your Brain With a Silent Stranger, CGP Grey's 2016 explainer of split-brain research, or The Egg - A Short Story, Kurzgesagt's 2019 animation. The long commitment is Ep. 1 - Awakening from the Meaning Crisis - Introduction, the opening of John Vervaeke's series on meaning and nihilism. Beyond those, the list covers Donald Hoffman on whether perception tracks reality, Anil Seth and Daniel Dennett at the Royal Institution, Joscha Bach on artificial consciousness, the Chomsky and Foucault debate on human nature, and Vedanta lectures from IIT Kanpur.

animals-nature.p1: This is less a nature roundup than a set of videos people reach for to settle a point. The Secret Reason Horses Let Us Ride Them is cited on Worldbuilding Stack Exchange whenever someone asks whether an invented creature could be domesticated or ridden. On Hacker News, Dominion (2018) - full documentary [Official] is pushed, sometimes hard, as the honest look at factory farming, and some say it changed how they eat. Dick Proenneke in Alone in the Wilderness comes up warmly in threads about cabins, solitude and woodworking, and DOUGLAS ADAMS: Parrots, the Universe and Everything is the talk Adams fans keep calling one of his best, funny and moving on extinction.
animals-nature.p2: For a quick first watch, try Two Monkeys Were Paid Unequally: Excerpt from Frans de Waal's TED Talk, a clip from his 2012 talk on moral behavior in animals, or the 2007 Attenborough lyre bird segment. The long commitment is Dominion, a full documentary, or the Siberian Happy People series, which viewers prefer in its original form over Herzog's shorter re-cut. Between those sit the BBC persistence hunting footage, Veritasium on trees, How Wolves Change Rivers, and a few strays like Kurzgesagt on nuclear accidents.

fitness-sleep-longevity.p1: Most of this list is about sleep, with fasting, breathing, exercise dosage and aging filling out the rest. Hacker News commenters post these as answers to questions that keep coming back: why am I always tired, how does fasting actually work, is more running always better. Master Your Sleep & Be More Alert When Awake is the one people credit with fixing their sleep, mainly through morning light and dimmer evenings. Guided Wim Hof Method Breathing is shared as a routine many report using daily for stress. Fasting For Survival Lecture by Dr Pradip Jamnadas and Joe Rogan Experience #1109 - Matthew Walker get cited as clear explanations of insulin and of Why We Sleep.
fitness-sleep-longevity.p2: For a first watch, Guided Wim Hof Method Breathing is something you follow along with rather than study. Fasting vs. Eating Less: What's the Difference? (Science of Fasting) from 2017 is a compact case for intermittent fasting. The bigger commitment is Dr. William Dement's 2008 Google TechTalk on sleep and performance, recommended on HN for years. Beyond that are a MedCram lecture on sunlight and melatonin, James O'Keefe's TEDx talk on moderate running, tendinitis exercises, Crash Course - The SMIDSY on motorcycle safety, and Kurzgesagt's Why Age? Should We End Aging Forever?

power-grid-heating.p1: This list is mostly answers to questions that keep coming up in home heating, appliance, and grid threads. Technology Connections dominates. Heat Pumps: the Future of Home Heating is the standard link when someone asks whether heat pumps work and why they are so efficient, and Portable Air Conditioners - Why you shouldn't like them gets posted on DIY Stack Exchange whenever someone asks about a portable unit. After every Texas grid failure, What Really Happened During the Texas Power Grid Outage? is cited as the calm technical account. James Burke Connections, Ep. 1 "The Trigger Effect" shows up in blackout threads as the classic case for how fragile interdependent systems are.
power-grid-heating.p2: Start with Heat Pumps: the Future of Home Heating from 2021. If it clicks, the 2022 follow-ups, Why Heat Pumps are Immensely Important Right Now and Heat Pumps are Not Hard, along with the geothermal episode, read as one series. The Burke episode is the bigger commitment, since it opens a whole series of its own. The rest covers black starts and connecting solar to the grid (Practical Engineering, 2024), gas stoves versus induction, electric kettles, Britain's peak demand, AC versus DC load breaking, and fan placement.

product-growth-marketing.p1: This is less a marketing course than a record of what people link when go-to-market questions come up. The most cited is Designing the Ideal Bootstrapped Business with Jason Cohen, the talk Hacker News hands to anyone weighing bootstrapping against venture money or puzzling over SaaS pricing. Much of the rest is skeptical. Facebook Fraud and its companion piece cover fake likes and bots. Tom Scott's This Video Is Sponsored By ███ VPN takes apart scare-tactic advertising, and Contrepreneurs: The Mikkelsen Twins covers passive-income hustles. A smaller set are plain answers, like Google Search Central explaining what to do with pages for discontinued products.
product-growth-marketing.p2: For a light first watch, try Joe Ades, Greatest Salesman in New York City History from 2008, which commenters treat as a lesson in how the way you sell matters more than what you sell. The Jason Cohen talk from 2019 is the one to set aside real time for. From there the list moves through platform critique in VidMe or Why Platforms Aren't Your Friends, Simon Sinek's Start with why talk in two versions, Veritasium on clickbait, and Adam Conover arguing that generational labels are marketing inventions.

nuclear-energy.p1: This list is mostly what Hacker News reaches for when a fusion headline lands or a nuclear power argument starts going in circles. The two most recommended videos are lectures that people cite to explain why high-temperature superconducting magnets changed the outlook for fusion: MIT's Pathway to Fusion Energy (IAP 2017) - Zach Hartwig and Breakthrough in Nuclear Fusion? - Prof. Dennis Whyte. Sabine Hossenfelder's How close is nuclear fusion power? gets posted under nearly every breakthrough story as a check on Q-factor hype. On the fission side, Economics of Nuclear Reactor answers the recurring question of why plants cost so much to build and comparatively little to run.
nuclear-energy.p2: Start with How close is nuclear fusion power? from 2021, the standard reality check. Kurzgesagt's Worst Nuclear Accidents in History is another good first watch, a compact overview comparing nuclear deaths with those from fossil fuels. The MIT fusion lectures from 2016 and 2017 are the bigger commitment and are worth a full sitting. The rest of the list covers thorium reactor advocacy from Google TechTalks in 2009 and 2011, pro-nuclear arguments from Bill Gates and Michael Shellenberger, and Helion's approach to fusion. It also includes Who Destroyed Three Mile Island?, a talk on systemic failure that commenters cite well outside nuclear threads.

earth-energy-other.p1: Most of this list is about limits: how fast energy use can grow, what happens when cheap oil runs out, and why energy transitions take decades. The anchor is Al Bartlett's lecture, posted twice here, including Arithmetic, Population and Energy - FULL LENGTH. Hacker News commenters keep quoting its thesis that humanity's greatest shortcoming is failing to understand the exponential function, even while noting that his peak oil forecasts missed. Alongside it sit talks people cite in arguments, such as Vaclav Smil's data-driven case against quick energy revolutions, The End of Suburbia - 52 minute documentary on peak oil, and the heavier How to Enjoy the End of the World.
earth-energy-other.p2: Start with America Was Wrong About Ethanol - Study Shows from 2022, an accessible summary of evidence that corn ethanol is no better than gasoline for emissions. Another good opener is NASA's Global Ocean Tides, which Physics Stack Exchange uses to show tides as resonant sloshing in ocean basins rather than two simple bulges. The long commitment is the full Bartlett lecture, then the 52 minute suburbia film. The rest mixes the Lake Peigneur drilling accident, John Oliver on coal, ExxonMobil lobbying, and two GIS tutorials.
